title: Cranky Kong Is The Original Donkey Kong
description: Fred Armisen's grumpy old ape Cranky Kong isn't just some random elder statesman of the Kong family. According to Mario lore, he's actually the very same Donkey Kong that squared off against Jumpman in the 1981 arcade game, just decades older and a lot crankier about it.

title: The DK Rap Makes The Cut
description: Donkey Kong's big entrance in the movie is scored to the DK Rap, the gloriously cheesy theme song from Donkey Kong 64 that's become a meme in its own right over the years. Oddly enough, the song's original composer Grant Kirkhope didn't get a credit for it in the film.

title: The Koopalings' Rock Band
description: During Bowser's rock concert scene, keep an eye on the band, because some of the Koopalings are up there performing. It's a nice touch given that in the English localisation of the games, several Koopalings are actually named after real musicians, including Iggy after Iggy Pop and Ludwig after Beethoven.

title: Bowser's Odyssey Wedding Suit
description: When Bowser finally gets his wedding scene, the tuxedo he's wearing is lifted straight from Super Mario Odyssey, where players could dress him up in his own wedding outfit during the Bowser's Kingdom segment. Fitting, really, considering how obsessed the guy is with marrying Peach across the games.

title: Royal Wedding Guest List
description: Bowser's wedding is packed with familiar faces if you look past the main cast. King Boo from Luigi's Mansion, King Bob-omb from Super Mario 64, and Petey Piranha from Super Mario Sunshine all show up in the crowd, three villains who probably shouldn't be on speaking terms with each other.

title: Gusty Garden Galaxy Plays The Movie Out
description: Stick around for the credits and you'll hear the Gusty Garden Galaxy theme from Super Mario Galaxy playing over the top, widely considered one of the best pieces of music Nintendo has ever put in a Mario game, so it's a genuinely lovely way to send the audience off.

title: Donkey Kong's First Redesign Since '94
description: The version of Donkey Kong you see swinging around in the movie is his first real design update since 1994. The filmmakers blended his classic, chunkier 1981 arcade look with the more modern proportions he's had since Donkey Kong Country to land somewhere in between.

title: Peach's More Hands-On Rescue
description: The directors were keen for Peach to feel like an actual ruler rather than someone waiting to be saved, and pulled a lot of that energy from her portrayal in Super Mario 3D World. Anya Taylor-Joy apparently leaned all the way into the role too, spending time playing through the games to get a feel for the character before recording.

title: Chris Pratt's Almost-Tony-Soprano Voice
description: Early in production, Chris Pratt tried out a voice for Mario that leaned much harder into a New Jersey accent. It ended up sounding so close to Tony Soprano that the directors had him dial it back and blend it more with the Italian-American, Brooklyn-flavoured voice that made it into the finished film.

title: Charlie Day's Goodfellas Phase
description: Chris Pratt wasn't the only one who had to dial back his voice work. Charlie Day originally recorded Luigi sounding a lot closer to a Goodfellas wiseguy before the directors steered him towards the softer, more anxious tone that ended up defining the character in the movie.

title: Jack Black's Chart-Topping Bowser Ballad
description: The directors decided it wasn't enough for Bowser to just tell Peach he loved her, he needed a whole song about it. Jack Black co-wrote and performed 'Peaches' for the film, and the track actually charted on the Billboard Hot 100, giving Black his first solo appearance on the chart after decades in music.

title: The Mario Family's Nintendo Sketches
description: Mario and Luigi's parents in the movie aren't the filmmakers' invention. Nintendo actually sent over unused character sketches for the wider Mario family, and the directors have said the dad's design is basically a one-to-one match for that original artwork, with the mum's design following pretty closely behind.

title: When Sony Nearly Beat Illumination To It
description: Years before Illumination got the rights, Sony was quietly trying to build its own Mario movie franchise. Emails leaked in the 2014 Sony hack revealed producer Avi Arad had met with Nintendo, and executive Amy Pascal had even floated Genndy Tartakovsky as a director, though it never got past early talks.

title: How Miyamoto And Illumination Actually Met
description: The whole movie arguably exists because of a theme park deal. Shigeru Miyamoto and Illumination founder Chris Meledandri first connected through Nintendo's partnership with Universal Parks on Super Nintendo World, and that relationship is what eventually grew into the pitch for an animated Mario film.

title: A Deliberately Different Approach To Teen Titans Go!
description: Directors Aaron Horvath and Michael Jelenic were best known beforehand for Teen Titans Go!, a show that took plenty of liberties with its source material and wasn't always loved by comic fans. This time round, they've said they deliberately went the opposite way, aiming for a genuinely faithful, cinematic take on Mario instead.

title: 85 References In One Movie
description: One outlet actually sat down and counted every single Nintendo reference they could find in the film, landing on a huge 85 separate Easter eggs, which works out to roughly one for every minute of runtime. Safe to say this is a movie built for repeat viewings.

title: Stan Lee Rides Every Train
description: Stan Lee's cameo in this one isn't just his little shop scene. The 180-odd animators on the film were all diehard Marvel fans and every single one of them wanted a shot at drawing him, so the directors let them sneak him in wherever they could. Pause the movie any time a subway train rattles past in the background and there's a very good chance you'll spot him sat inside it. It ended up being his last ever voice role.

title: Aunt May's Oscar Pedigree
description: Lily Tomlin voicing Aunt May keeps a weirdly specific streak going. Rosemary Harris, Sally Field and Marisa Tomei all played May in live action and all picked up Oscar nominations at some point in their careers, and Tomlin herself was nominated for Nashville decades earlier. The writers apparently had her in mind the whole time they were writing this tougher, more no-nonsense version of the character.

title: The Leap of Faith Was Never Cut
description: The shot everyone remembers, Miles stepping off the building and finally trusting himself as he swings off into the city, was there from the very first draft of the script. It never got rewritten out or reworked into something else, it just stayed the emotional center of the whole movie and became the backbone of the marketing too.

title: Seventy Attempts to Turn Invisible
description: Miles' invisibility power sounds simple on paper, but figuring out how it should actually look on screen was a nightmare for the animation team. They went through around 70 different visual designs trying to nail down something that felt cool without looking like a generic vanishing effect, before landing on the version that made it into the final cut.

title: Cage Channeled Bogart for Noir
description: Nicolas Cage grew up reading comics, so getting a call about Spider-Man Noir was a dream gig for him, especially once the filmmakers told him to just have fun with it. Since Noir is a hard-boiled 1930s detective rendered in black and white, Cage leaned on Humphrey Bogart for the clipped, fast-talking delivery, figuring it would land with both noir fans and kids discovering the genre for the first time.

title: A Month for Four Seconds of Footage
description: The comic-book look wasn't just a filter slapped over the CG. Every rendered frame got a hand-drawn pass from an artist afterward, and the directors wouldn't allow any panels, sound-effect lettering or word balloons on screen until after Miles gets bitten. On a normal animated film a team can knock out four seconds of footage in a week. Here it took roughly a month.

title: The Christmas Album Almost Never Happened
description: That running gag about Peter Parker releasing a cheesy holiday album, complete with titles like a mistletoe-themed swing anthem, wasn't planned from the start. Phil Lord and Christopher Miller dreamed it up while the film was already being scored, and only found out Chris Pine could actually sing when he showed up and nailed the recording session.

title: Spider-Ham's Filthy First Takes
description: This was John Mulaney's first role in a theatrically released movie, and the producers told him to just play around in the booth. He took that a little too literally at first, ad-libbing a string of curse words as Spider-Ham before finally stopping to ask what rating they were going for. Once he found out it was a family film, he dialed it right back.

title: The Divorce That Almost Was
description: Peter B. Parker going through a messy split from Mary Jane is actually a nod to an unmade Sam Raimi script. Raimi had once planned for Peter and MJ to be married and later divorced in a fourth live-action film, after Peter's affair with Felicia Hardy came to light. Raimi eventually backed away from that storyline because it made Peter too unlikeable, and the project got shelved when Sony wouldn't give him time for a rewrite. This film quietly resurrects the idea as a joke.

title: Built Around Shameik Moore's Performance
description: Co-director Rodney Rothman has said a huge chunk of how Miles moves and feels came directly from Shameik Moore's voice work. Moore landed the role after one set of dialogue tests, and he wasn't just reading lines, he was bringing unscripted emotion and body language that the animators then built the character's physical performance around.

title: Miles Moves Slower Than Everyone Else
description: The film runs at the standard 24 frames per second, but a lot of the character animation is done on twos, meaning a new drawing only every other frame, which drops the effective rate to 12. Early in the movie this is used specifically on Miles, so before he's found his footing as Spider-Man he visibly moves with less grace than the other Spider-people, who are animated more smoothly.

title: No Motion Blur, Just Hand-Drawn Smears
description: Instead of the usual photorealistic motion blur you'd get in modern CG, the animation team drew old-school smear frames by hand to sell fast movement, the same trick classic 2D cartoons used decades ago. It keeps every pose looking like a clean illustration rather than a blurry photograph, which is a big part of why the action reads like it's ripped straight off a comic page.

title: Blurry Edges Look Like a Misprinted Comic
description: Watch anything that's slightly out of focus in the background and you'll notice it splitting into little red, green and blue fringes, mimicking chromatic aberration. It's a deliberate wink at old comic books, which often had their ink layers slightly misaligned during printing, and it's subtle enough that a lot of people watch the whole film without consciously clocking it.

title: Kingpin Is Drawn From a 1986 Comic
description: This version of Wilson Fisk isn't based on any of his earlier film appearances. His look is pulled from the 1986 graphic novel Daredevil: Love and War, illustrated by Bill Sienkiewicz, which is also where the film gets the softer, more devoted side of Fisk's relationship with his wife Vanessa before it all curdles into obsession.

title: Cast Around a Broken Leg
description: Liev Schreiber was actually the second actor locked in for the movie, right after Nicolas Cage. The filmmakers tested their early Kingpin designs against old line readings of Schreiber from Ray Donovan to see if the voice would fit, and co-director Bob Persichetti later joked that the week Schreiber finally called to accept happened to be the same week he broke his leg.

title: Green Goblin Grew 22 Feet Tall
description: Forget the guy in a purple suit and glider from other adaptations. This Green Goblin takes his cue from the more monstrous version found in the Ultimate Spider-Man comics, ending up as a hulking, scaly, 22-foot-tall creature with a purple tongue rather than anything resembling a costume.

title: Tombstone Was Designed as a Zombie
description: Kingpin's enforcer Tombstone got a deliberately eerie makeover for this film. The artists pitched him as a kind of giant zombie, meant to work as a visual counterpart to the 1930s noir stylings of Spider-Man Noir, since both characters draw from that same vintage, monochrome era of pulp fiction.

title: Sunflower Was Plan B
description: The song playing when we first meet Miles almost wasn't Sunflower at all. The filmmakers had a different track locked in for that scene until the rights fell through, leaving them scrambling to find a replacement in time to still animate the shot around it. Post Malone and Swae Lee's song ended up working even better than the original plan, since the joke was always that Miles is singing something a little out of his depth, which mirrors him being handed a role he doesn't feel ready for.

title: Sunflower Tied a Billboard Record
description: Sunflower went on to spend 33 weeks inside the Billboard Hot 100's top ten, tying the record held at the time by Maroon 5 and Cardi B's Girls Like You and Ed Sheeran's Shape of You. Not bad for a song that was only added to the movie after the original choice fell apart.

title: Peni Parker's Anime Glow-Up
description: The bubbly, anime-inspired take on Peni Parker that this movie made popular is actually a pretty big departure from her original comic version, who was written as much more solemn and serious. This film's cheerier, more genki-girl interpretation ended up sticking so hard that it shaped how she's been written ever since, showing up again in the sequel and later in games like Marvel Rivals.

title: Breaking Disney and Pixar's Grip on the Oscar
description: When this film took home the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, it beat out Incredibles 2, Isle of Dogs, Mirai and Ralph Breaks the Internet, and it did it as a film with no Pixar or Disney involvement, something that had really only happened before with DreamWorks' Shrek and Rango.

title: Peter Ramsey Made Oscar History
description: Co-director Peter Ramsey became the first African-American director to win an Academy Award in the Best Animated Feature category, sharing the win with fellow directors Bob Persichetti and Rodney Rothman alongside producers Phil Lord and Christopher Miller.

title: A $90 Million Bet That Paid Off
description: Made on a $90 million budget, the film wasn't a guaranteed hit going in, since it was the first fully animated Spider-Man movie and had to win over both newcomers and comic-book purists at the same time. It ended up grossing nearly $375 million worldwide and opened to $35.4 million domestically, which set a record for the biggest opening weekend ever for an animated film released in December.

title: The First Afro-Latino Spider-Man on Screen
description: Miles Morales here became the first Afro-Latino incarnation of Spider-Man to headline mainstream media, carrying a Puerto Rican mother and African American father into a character who'd previously only existed on the big screen as Peter Parker.

title: Cupcakes Are a Caitlyn Callback
description: Right at the start of episode one, when Vi, Mylo, Powder and Claggor are legging it across the rooftops, Claggor grabs a cupcake off a tray mid-heist. Looks like a throwaway gag, but that exact cupcake trap is Caitlyn's in-game ability Yordle Snap Trap, icon and all. Vi even calls Caitlyn 'Cupcake' as a nickname later in the show, so the whole thing loops back around nicely.

title: Powder's Sketchbook Hides a Skin Reference
description: In episode three, while Powder's sat crying next to her drawings, you can spot a crude sketch of a pair of pink-outlined wings among the doodles of Fishbones and dynamite. That's a nod to Star Guardian Jinx, one of her flashier in-game skins, tucked into the show years before most viewers would've clocked it.

title: Teemo Is Hiding Everywhere
description: Teemo never shows up as an actual character, but he's absolutely everywhere if you look. He's on an arcade cabinet Powder plays in episode two, he's in a children's book one of Silco's men waves around to scare a kid, and by season two his signature scout helmet is basically Isha's whole look. Sevika's mechanical arm even nods to him. The little Yordle gets more screen time in references than most named cast members.

title: That Horned Helmet in Benzo's Shop
description: Hanging above the door in Benzo's shop is a big horned helmet that fans immediately clocked as Tryndamere's headgear from his original in-game skin. He never turns up in person, but it's a nice little wink for anyone who's spent time on Summoner's Rift.

title: Krugs Show Up Before the Show Even Aired
description: The jungle monsters Krugs get an odd little cameo when Ekko and the other kids are seen poking at a cluster of them. Funnily enough, this exact same critter turned up in the 'Enemy' music video that dropped before Arcane even premiered, so eagle-eyed junglers spotted the reference before the show had aired a single episode.

title: An Esports Wheel Hidden in the Alternate Universe
description: During episode seven of season two, while Ekko is wandering through the alternate universe, there's a carnival game in the background with a spinning wheel painted with real esports team logos, including T1, Gen.G and Fnatic. Blink and you'll genuinely miss it.

title: Orianna's Statue Is a Spoiler in Plain Sight
description: When Singed visits the room set aside for his daughter, there's a ballerina statue sitting there that looks a lot like Orianna's eventual champion design. Sure enough, later in the season she shows up in a fully mechanical body, hinting Viktor may have had a hand in rebuilding her.

title: A Three-Eyed Crow Is Teasing Swain
description: Swain never appears on screen in Arcane, but a black crow with three eyes is shown flying over the rubble of Piltover and later among the Noxian ships. That's the exact crow from Swain's official splash art, and most fans read it as a not-so-subtle hint that Noxus could be next for the League of Legends TV treatment.

title: Janna Watches Over the Zaun Miners
description: Season two slips in a wind spirit protecting the Zaun miners who never gets named on screen, but her design and role line up with Janna, the storm-guardian champion from the game. It's the kind of blink-and-you-miss-it cameo that only really lands if you already know the lore.

title: Young Jayce Was Saved by a Ryze Cameo
description: There's a moment where a cloaked, mysterious mage saves a young Jayce, and the spell effect used looks suspiciously like Ryze's Realm Warp ability from the game. It's one of the more obscure references in the whole series, easy to miss unless you're specifically looking for it.

title: Vander Was Warwick All Along
description: That fan theory going around since season one turned out to be spot on. Singed brings Vander back from the brink after his fight with Silco by turning him into Warwick, the feral beast champion. According to the animation team, the idea that Vander's stubborn resilience would eventually make him into Warwick was baked into the character from the very start of the show.

title: Ambessa Drops a Kindred Hint
description: In the final act, as Ambessa is about to lose to Mel, she calls her 'the Wolf' right before things go south. It's a small line, but plenty of fans think it's pointing toward Kindred, the champion literally made up of a wolf and a lamb, suggesting Mel might have a bigger role to play in whatever comes after Arcane.

title: Silco Raised the Girl Piltover Feared Most
description: After Vi is arrested and Powder is left alone following the tunnel explosion, it's Silco who takes her in and shapes her into Jinx. He's framed as a villain for most of the run, but the show is careful to make his bond with her feel genuine, which is exactly what makes the ending hurt as much as it does.

title: Hextech Is the Spark That Splits the City
description: Pretty much everything in Arcane traces back to Hextech, the invention Jayce and Viktor create to let ordinary people harness magical energy. It's meant to be a great equaliser, but instead it becomes the thing that widens the gap between wealthy Piltover and the neglected undercity of Zaun even further.

title: It Took Six Years to Get Arcane to Screen
description: Co-creators Christian Linke and Alex Yee have said the whole project took around six years from start to finish, meaning work on it stretches back to roughly 2015. A lot of the cast weren't nearly as famous back then as they are now, which makes the eventual voice lineup feel like a bit of a lucky break in hindsight.

title: Fortiche Started Out Making Adverts
description: The French studio behind Arcane's whole look, Fortiche, was set up back in 2009 by three friends, Jérôme Combe, Pascal Charrue and Arnaud Delord. Before they ever touched an animated series, they were making commercials for the likes of Coca-Cola and Samsung, then moved into music videos, with a Gorillaz collaboration being their big early break.

title: 450 Artists Worked on Season Two
description: At the busiest point of production on season two, Fortiche had roughly 450 artists working across studios in the US and France, covering everything from character animation to matte paintings and lighting. Riot Games' co-director Barthelemy Maunoury has described the working relationship with Linke as going back over a decade at that point.

title: Arcane Made Emmy History Twice
description: Season one made Arcane the first streaming show ever to win the Emmy for Outstanding Animated Program, back in 2022, and it took home four wins total that year. Season two then repeated the trick in 2025, beating out competition like Bob's Burgers and The Simpsons for the same award.

title: Arcane Swept the Annie Awards
description: Between its two seasons, Arcane became the first TV series to sweep the Annie Awards in a single year, and it later racked up seven wins at the 52nd Annies for season two alone, more than any other nominated show that year including Dream Productions.

title: 'Enemy' Was Riot's Second Team-Up With Imagine Dragons
description: Imagine Dragons and JID's theme song 'Enemy' wasn't the band's first rodeo with Riot Games. They'd already made 'Warriors' back in 2014 for the League of Legends World Championship, so by the time Arcane rolled around it was a bit of a reunion rather than a first date.

title: 'Enemy' Cracked the Billboard Hot 100 Top 10
description: The Arcane theme song didn't just do well for a TV tune, it genuinely blew up. 'Enemy' hit number one on Billboard's Top TV Songs chart, climbed into the Hot 100's top 10, and gave JID his first ever top five single in the US.

title: Arcane Knocked Squid Game Off the Top Spot
description: Within just three days of dropping, Arcane had already dethroned Squid Game as the most-watched show on Netflix worldwide, debuting at number one in 37 countries. Not bad for a show based on a video game most non-players had never even heard of.

title: Season Two Beat Season One's Numbers by a Mile
description: According to Netflix's own engagement reports, season two racked up 234 million hours watched in its first 28 days, well ahead of season one's 166 million over the same window. That makes it one of the biggest jumps in viewership between seasons for any Netflix original.

title: Season Two Reportedly Cost $250 Million
description: Arcane's second season carried a reported budget of around $250 million, which puts it up there as one of the most expensive animated series ever produced. Given how hand-crafted the animation is, with animators acting out scenes themselves rather than relying on shortcuts, it's not exactly a shock.

title: Casting News Landed the Same Day as Hawkeye's Trailer
description: When Riot Games announced the Arcane voice cast in September 2021, it happened to land on the exact same day as the trailer for Marvel's Hawkeye, which stars Hailee Steinfeld, the same actor voicing Vi. Total coincidence, but it made for a pretty big week for her.

title: JB Blanc Voices Both Vander and Warwick
description: JB Blanc doesn't just voice Vander, he also plays Warwick once the transformation happens, meaning the same actor carries the character all the way through his tragic arc from father figure to feral weapon.

title: Fortiche's Animators Acted Out the Fights Themselves
description: Rather than lean on motion capture or shortcuts, Fortiche's animators regularly filmed themselves acting out scenes with household props standing in for guns and hammers, then used that footage as reference. It's part of why the fights and small facial moments feel so lived-in rather than stiff.

title: Recast After a Real Tragedy
description: Uncle Iroh was voiced by Mako Iwamatsu for the first two seasons, but Mako passed away from cancer in the middle of production. Greg Baldwin, who'd been doing scratch dialogue and impressions of Mako for years, stepped in to finish out Book Three so the character wouldn't have to change entirely.

title: A Goodbye Hidden Inside a Filler Episode
description: In 'The Tales of Ba Sing Se,' Iroh spends the whole episode quietly helping strangers before we find out why: it's his son Lu Ten's birthday, and Lu Ten died taking the city years earlier. Iroh sings 'Leaves From the Vine' through tears, and the segment closes on a dedication to Mako, who died just before the episode aired. It's considered by a lot of fans to be the saddest moment in the whole show.

title: Toph Was Almost a Guy
description: Before Toph Beifong became the blind, sarcastic earthbending prodigy we know, the character was originally written as male. Bits of that original design apparently still float around the show in background characters, including the wrestler known as The Boulder.

title: The Bending Styles Are Real Kung Fu
description: None of the fighting in the show was made up from scratch. Waterbending is built on Tai Chi Chuan, earthbending on Hung Gar, firebending on Northern Shaolin, and airbending on Baguazhang, with Toph getting her own flavor pulled from Southern Praying Mantis. The show's animators actually studied footage of these styles to get the movement right.

title: One Guy Choreographed Every Fight
description: Martial arts consultant Sifu Kisu worked on all 61 episodes of the original series. He'd physically act out each fight so the animators had real reference footage to draw from, which is a big part of why the bending choreography still holds up so well.

title: Earthbending Was Never a Human Invention
description: In-universe, humans didn't invent earthbending at all. The show's mythology credits the blind badger moles as the original earthbenders, with the two lovers who founded Omashu learning the art by watching the moles dig their tunnels.

title: Capoeira Snuck Into a Fire Nation Dance Scene
description: Not every movement in the show is Chinese martial arts. The dancing in Season 3's 'The Headband' was actually based on capoeira, the Brazilian style that blends fighting with dance, giving that one scene a completely different rhythm from anything else in the series.

title: A Sneaky Terminator Reference
description: Master swordsman Piandao is voiced by Robert Patrick, best known for playing the liquid-metal T-1000 in Terminator 2. The writers apparently couldn't resist giving Piandao a throwaway line connecting the two roles, a little wink for anyone who catches it.

title: Toph Basically Drew the Nickelodeon Logo
description: Keep an eye on Toph's metalbending in Book Three and you might catch her twisting metal into a splat-like shape that mirrors the Nickelodeon logo, minus the lettering. It's such a quick gag that most people watch right past it.

title: Ba Sing Se Is Basically the Forbidden City
description: The massive walled capital of the Earth Kingdom wasn't dreamed up from nothing. The creators modeled its layout and architecture directly on Beijing's Forbidden City, which is a big part of why Ba Sing Se feels so imposing and layered compared to the show's smaller towns.

title: It All Started With an Old Doodle
description: Co-creator Bryan Konietzko has said the whole idea began with a much older sketch he'd drawn of a balding, middle-aged bald man. He got curious about what that same man might've looked like as a kid, drew him herding a bison, and that image ended up being the seed for Aang and Appa.

title: Made in South Korea, Written in Burbank
description: The show was written and produced out of Nickelodeon's studio in Burbank, but almost all the actual animation was outsourced to South Korean studios JM Animation, DR Movie, and MOI Animation, which is fairly standard for American TV animation but not something most viewers ever think about.

title: A Kids' Cartoon That Won a Peabody
description: Avatar: The Last Airbender took home a Peabody Award in 2008, an honor usually reserved for serious journalism and prestige drama. For a Nickelodeon action-adventure cartoon aimed at kids, that's a pretty rare shelf to sit on.

title: The Score Uses Instruments You've Probably Never Heard
description: Composers Jeremy Zuckerman and Benjamin Wynn deliberately avoided the usual animation-composer playbook, instead learning to work with instruments like the guzheng, the pipa, and the duduk to match the show's Asian-inspired world. That's a big reason the soundtrack sounds nothing like a typical 2000s Nickelodeon show.

title: An Invader Zim Cameo on the Ba Sing Se Tram
description: Right after Sokka mutters that weird stuff keeps happening to the group, a guy sucking on an ear of corn sits down near him and Toph on the Ba Sing Se tram. Fans have long pointed to it as a nod to Invader Zim, another Nickelodeon show with its own devoted cult following.

title: What 'Ran' and 'Shaw' Actually Mean
description: The last two dragons Aang and Zuko meet aren't named randomly. Ran roughly translates to 'burn' or 'ignite' in Chinese, and Shaw carries a similar meaning around blazing or combustion, which fits since the pair end up teaching the boys that firebending doesn't have to come from rage.

title: Iroh Lied to Save the Species
description: For years, everyone in the Fire Nation believed Iroh when he claimed to have killed the last dragon, a story that made him a war hero. It turns out he made the whole thing up to protect Ran and Shaw, the two remaining dragons hidden away by the Sun Warriors, letting the world think the species was extinct.

title: The Cabbage Merchant Made It Into Baldur's Gate 3
description: The Cabbage Vendor's whole shtick of watching his cart get destroyed became such a running joke that it escaped the franchise entirely. He shows up in Baldur's Gate 3, complete with an extra bit of dialogue reserved just for Monk characters.

title: The Pilot Nickelodeon Turned Down
description: Before Cartoon Network ever touched it, Pendleton Ward actually pitched an Adventure Time pilot to Nickelodeon back in 2008. They passed on it. It wasn't until the original short blew up online that Cartoon Network came knocking a year later, and the rest is history.

title: Jake Was Basically Bill Murray
description: Jake's whole laid-back, do-whatever-feels-right vibe wasn't pulled from thin air. Pendleton Ward has said he based the character on Tripper Harrison, Bill Murray's slacker camp counselor from the 1979 comedy Meatballs, right down to the way Jake will drop the goofiness and give Finn real advice when it actually matters.

title: The Creator Is Lumpy Space Princess
description: That whiny, dramatic voice you hear every time LSP shows up on screen belongs to none other than Pendleton Ward himself. He also does a handful of other side characters like Shelby and the Snow Golem, but LSP is the one that stuck as his signature role in his own show.

title: The War That Built Ooo
description: Everything weird and colorful about the Land of Ooo exists because of a global nuclear exchange the show calls the Mushroom War, which happened roughly a thousand years before Finn and Jake ever met. It wiped out most of humanity, physically reshaped the planet, and somehow left behind a world of sentient candy people and elemental kingdoms in its place.

title: The Timeline Where Simon Saves The World
description: In the alternate Farmworld reality shown in "Finn the Human" and "Jake the Dog," Finn wishes the Lich never existed, and it rewrites history so that Simon Petrikov froze the mushroom bomb solid in midair before it could detonate, sacrificing his own life in the process. It's a rare glimpse at what Ooo could've looked like if the apocalypse had been stopped.

title: The Snail That Waves At You
description: Keep your eyes peeled in the background of almost every single episode and you'll spot a tiny snail somewhere in the frame, usually waving right at the camera. It started as a silent running gag from the animators, but the show eventually gave it actual plot relevance when the Lich possesses it to escape the amber prison.

title: A Crown Older Than The Ice King Himself
description: Ice King's crown wasn't made for him at all. The show eventually reveals it was forged way back in the Mesozoic Era by an ice elemental named Urgence Evergreen, meant to stop an evil version of the catalyst comet from wiping out life on Earth. Simon Petrikov just happened to be the poor guy who found it centuries later in a Scandinavian dockyard.

title: The Man Behind Ice King
description: Before he was rambling about princesses and penguins, Ice King was a scholar named Simon Petrikov, engaged to a woman called Betty Grof. He found a strange crown on an expedition to Scandinavia, and wearing it slowly ate away at his memories and sanity until Simon disappeared entirely, leaving the deranged wizard fans grew up watching.

title: Betty's Final Sacrifice
description: In the series finale, Betty finally manages to cure Simon by using his own crown against the cosmic being GOLB, but the wish comes at a cost. She ends up permanently fusing with GOLB herself, giving Simon back his humanity while she disappears from Ooo for good.

title: Jake And Bender Share A Voice
description: John DiMaggio doesn't just voice Jake the Dog, he's also the guy behind Bender in Futurama, and honestly you can hear a bit of Bender's swagger in Jake's delivery. The connection got a fun little nod when Finn and Jake popped up for a quick cameo in the Futurama episode "Leela and the Genestalk."

title: Marceline Left A Mark On Her Voice Actor
description: Olivia Olson clearly loves the character she plays, because she has Marceline's iconic Ax Bass tattooed right on her wrist. It's the kind of detail that makes you realize just how much some of these voice actors genuinely bonded with their roles over the years.

title: Marceline's Dad Is Voiced By Her Real Dad
description: There's a nice bit of real-life family casting hidden in the show. Olivia Olson's adoptive father, Martin Olson, who was also a writer on Phineas and Ferb, provides the voice of Hunson Abadeer, Marceline's demon dad and Lord of the Nightosphere.

title: How Tom Kenny Already Knew Marceline
description: Tom Kenny, who voices Ice King, actually met Olivia Olson when she was just a baby, since he used to perform stand-up comedy at her father Martin Olson's club. Years later they'd end up sharing scenes together as two of the show's most beloved characters.

title: Ice King's Cringeworthy Search History
description: There's a blink-and-you'll-miss-it moment where Ice King's computer screen shows off his actual browser history, and it's full of pathetic, oddly specific searches about handling princesses and strange health questions. It's a tiny detail but it adds a whole extra layer of sadness to how lonely the guy really is underneath the jokes.

title: The Population Chart Hidden In High Strangeness
description: Pause the right frame during "High Strangeness" in season 8 and you'll catch a background world population chart that shows just how brutal the Mushroom War really was, with a population crash on the scale of a full world war. There's even a tiny dip earlier on the chart referencing the Black Plague, which is a wild amount of detail for something most people will never notice.

title: Gunter Was The Biggest Foreshadow All Along
description: Way back in an early season, a throwaway line identifies Gunter as the most evil thing certain characters had ever encountered, and at the time it plays as a silly joke. Turns out it was quietly setting up one of the show's biggest cosmic reveals, since Gunter is secretly the ancient being Orgalorg.

title: Finn's Backpack Has A Dora Connection
description: Finn's green backpack occasionally shows a little bit of personality and even interacts with him, which is a subtle wink at Dora the Explorer's talking backpack. It's a small joke, but once you notice it you can't unsee it.

title: The Candy Kingdom's Guards Look Familiar
description: The Banana Guards protecting the Candy Kingdom share a suspicious amount of DNA with the Minions from Despicable Me, both in their yellow, rounded shape and their goofy group energy. It's never called out directly in the show, but the resemblance is hard to miss once you're looking for it.

title: Why Pendleton Ward Stepped Back
description: Pendleton Ward only ran the show as showrunner for its first couple of seasons before handing the reins over to Adam Muto. He's talked about how the pressure of running a hit series basically overwhelmed him, and stepping back let him stay involved as a producer without burning out completely.

title: Tree Trunks Died, Then She Didn't
description: For a while, Pendleton Ward flat out told fans that Tree Trunks was definitely dead. Then the episode "Crystals Have Power" rolled around and quietly walked that back, bringing her into play again like nothing ever happened. Ice King's age got the same treatment, jumping around over the years depending on what the story needed.

title: BMO's Space Trip Is Full Of Movie Nods
description: The Distant Lands special "BMO" leans hard into classic sci-fi and fantasy references. When BMO and Olive travel through the Drift, the colorful lights are a direct homage to 2001: A Space Odyssey, and if you look closely at BMO's insides, there's a tiny medal and diploma tucked next to their heart, mirroring the gifts the Wizard gives to the Tin Man and Scarecrow in The Wizard of Oz.

title: BMO's Donut Line Is A Real Old Ad
description: When BMO says "time to make the donuts" before getting to work in the Distant Lands special, it's not an original BMO catchphrase. It's a straight lift from a Dunkin' Donuts commercial character from the 1980s, dropped in as a little treat for older viewers watching alongside their kids.

title: Old Faces Sneak Into Fionna And Cake
description: The Fionna and Cake episode "Cake the Cat" is stuffed with callbacks for longtime fans, including a cameo from Minerva, who first showed up during the original finale's closing montage, and a background appearance from the two-headed duck pulled straight from the original show's opening title sequence.

title: Marshall Lee's Guitar Case Is A Punk Playlist
description: Look closely at the stickers plastered on Marshall Lee's guitar case in Fionna and Cake and you'll spot a bunch of cheeky riffs on real punk band names, like X-Ray Pex standing in for X-Ray Spex and Daikini Kill standing in for Bikini Kill. It's a fun little detail for anyone who grew up on that scene.

title: That Old Please Stand By Screen
description: Right at the start of episode one, Vault 33's monitors flash up that familiar 'Please Stand By' card before the wedding kicks off. It's the same holding screen the games have used for decades on their loading and title screens, so if you've ever booted up a Fallout game you'll have seen this exact graphic staring back at you before.

title: The Vault Cameras Cut To Static Mid-Massacre
description: When raiders storm Vault 33 and things turn violent, the internal broadcast system that's been playing that cheery propaganda footage actually glitches out and falls back to the 'Please Stand By' card again, this time as the wedding descends into chaos behind it. Nice bit of visual irony from the production team.

title: Stimpaks Look Exactly Like The Games
description: After the wedding turns into a bloodbath, the survivors reach for Stimpaks to patch themselves up, and the props team clearly did their homework because the syringes are basically lifted straight from the games, right down to the shape and the needle design. Small touch, but fans noticed immediately.

title: Snip-Snip Is Voiced By A What We Do In The Shadows Star
description: The unsettling Mr. Handy unit that specialises in reattaching limbs (and taking a few in the process) is called Snip-Snip, and he's voiced by Matt Berry, best known for playing the vampire Laszlo on What We Do in the Shadows. His unmistakable voice makes the robot even creepier once you clock who's behind it.

title: The Man Behind Codsworth's Voice
description: Episode six reveals that Matt Berry's character, the actor who did all those Mr. Handy voiceovers pre-war, was actually a man called Sebastian Leslie. He and Cooper Howard knew each other in old Hollywood, and Sebastian had signed away the rights to his voice, which is why it ended up echoing out of household robots for the next two centuries.

title: The Bridge Fiends Are Straight Out Of New Vegas
description: The hollow-eyed raiders that Maximus and Lucy scrap with on the bridge aren't just generic bandits, they're Fiends, a chem-addicted faction that made their debut in Fallout: New Vegas. In the games they're famous for attacking anything that moves, and the show keeps that same feral, no-negotiation energy.

title: Shady Sands Used To Be A Big Deal
description: The ruined settlement of Shady Sands that keeps popping up in flashbacks isn't just set dressing, it was once the capital of the New California Republic and the largest post-war settlement in the original two Fallout games. Seeing it wiped off the map in the show is a genuinely heavy moment for anyone who's followed the series that long.

title: That Airship Has A Sneaky Double Reference
description: The massive airship the Brotherhood of Steel rolls up in looks like a dead ringer for the Prydwen from Fallout 4, and the show even nods to where that name came from, since it's named after King Arthur's ship in an old Welsh poem. In the series it's given the name Caswennan, which is another name tied to that same legendary vessel.

title: Young Maximus And The Fridge
description: There's a moment where a young Maximus survives a nuclear blast by climbing into a fridge, and eagle-eyed fans reckon it's a wink at the Fallout 4 side quest 'Kid in a Fridge,' where the player rescues a super mutant kid who's been hiding out in an old refrigerator for who knows how long.

title: YumYum Deviled Eggs Made The Jump To Live Action
description: Keep an eye out on the tables and shelves throughout the wasteland and you'll spot tins of YumYum Deviled Eggs, a health-boosting snack that's been a staple food item in the games since Fallout 3. It's the kind of background prop that only really lands if you've spent hours digging through in-game inventories.

title: War Never Changes, Twice In The Finale
description: The franchise's signature line gets a proper callback in the season one finale, first spoken by Barb during the Vault-Tec conspiracy meeting, then echoed two hundred years later by Cooper, who's clearly quoting her without the audience even realising it until that second use lands.

title: The Show Is Set Further Into The Future Than Any Game
description: Fallout the show doesn't retell any single game's story, it jumps ahead to 2296, which makes it the furthest point in the timeline the franchise has ever shown. That means every mainline Fallout game technically happened before the events we're watching, and the show treats all of it as settled canon rather than just inspiration.

title: Jet Shows Up Early And Often
description: The raiders in episode one, including the Ghoul himself, are seen using Jet, the highly addictive inhalant drug that's been part of Fallout's chem lineup for years. It's a subtle bit of characterisation as much as an easter egg, since Jet use has always been shorthand in the games for someone who's rough around the edges.

title: Season 2's Poster Is Hiding The Whole Vegas Strip
description: Squint at the season two poster and you can pick out the Lucky 38, Mr. House's iconic tower from Fallout: New Vegas, sitting in the background haze. Fans have also spotted what looks like The Tops and a sliver of Gomorrah tucked into the skyline, so the marketing team was clearly having fun rewarding people who know their Strip casinos.

title: They Deliberately Didn't Adapt One Specific Game
description: Jonathan Nolan has said outright that the writers never wanted to just retell one of the existing games beat for beat. Because every Fallout game already tells its own self-contained story in a different city, the team decided the show would earn its place by doing the same thing rather than adapting an existing plot.

title: Production Kicked Off In The Summer Of 2022
description: Cameras started rolling on the series back in June 2022, with filming spread across New Jersey, New York, and Utah. Some of the earliest behind-the-scenes shots that leaked online were from a Super Duper Mart set built on Staten Island, a location name that longtime players will recognise instantly.

title: Walton Goggins Sat In The Chair For Five Hours A Day
description: Turning into the Ghoul wasn't a quick job, at least not at first. Walton Goggins originally spent up to five hours in makeup every single day to become the character, with prosthetics designer Jake Garber gradually whittling that process down over time as they both got more efficient at it.

title: The Ghoul Needed Nine Separate Prosthetic Pieces
description: Goggins' transformation into the Ghoul wasn't one mask, it was nine individual prosthetic pieces applied in sequence, along with a punishing daily prep schedule. He's since described the whole ritual as genuinely nerve-wracking, especially in the early days before the process was refined.

title: The Nose Removal Is The One CGI Cheat
description: Almost everything about the Ghoul's look is done practically with prosthetics, but there's one exception. Goggins' nose is digitally removed in post-production, since that was the one detail the team couldn't quite pull off convincingly with makeup alone while still letting him act naturally under the rest of the prosthetic work.

title: Goggins Avoided The Games On Purpose
description: Rather than boning up on the source material, Walton Goggins deliberately steered clear of playing the Fallout games before stepping into the role, choosing instead to build the Ghoul's persona from classic Western films, drawing on the kind of weathered gunslinger energy you'd get from John Wayne or Clint Eastwood.

title: The Wasteland Is Actually Namibia
description: A lot of that sun-scorched, dune-covered wasteland footage wasn't built on a soundstage, it's the real Skeleton Coast in Namibia. The crew leaned on the natural desert landscape rather than heavy CGI, which is a big part of why the wasteland feels so tangible and lived-in compared to a lot of other big-budget shows.

title: A Real Shipwreck Ended Up On Screen
description: One of the eerier backdrops Lucy walks past while exploring the surface is the actual wreck of the Eduard Bohlen, a German cargo ship that ran aground on Namibia's coast back in 1909 and has been slowly swallowed by sand ever since. No set dressing needed, it was already sitting there looking perfectly post-apocalyptic.

title: Red Rocket Was Built From Scratch In Three Days
description: The Red Rocket truck stop that shows up in the episode 'The Radio' is a genuine easter egg for players, since it's the exact type of gas station where you first meet Dogmeat in Fallout 4. To pull it off, the crew transformed a real petrol station in Nyack, New York into the iconic red-and-white design in just three days.

title: The Brotherhood's Base Has A Hollywood Resume
description: The Brotherhood of Steel's headquarters was filmed at Wendover Airfield in Utah, a genuine WWII-era base that's now a museum. It's not the show's first brush with fame either, the same airfield has previously turned up in Con Air, Independence Day, and Ang Lee's Hulk.

title: Season 3 Is Officially Happening
description: Amazon confirmed Fallout would return for a third season, announcing the renewal ahead of season two's launch. By that point the first two seasons had already pulled in over 100 million viewers worldwide between them, landing among the most-watched seasons in Prime Video's history.

title: Todd Howard Has Been Living In This World For Over A Decade
description: Bethesda's Todd Howard came on board as an executive producer, bringing over ten years of history with the franchise as both director and producer on the games themselves. Having him in the room helped keep the show's tone and world-building honest to what longtime players already know.

title: New Vegas Got Rebuilt In North Hollywood
description: For season two, production shifted away from Namibia and New York entirely, relocating to California so the team could recreate the neon ruins of New Vegas. The shift also let the crew build out locations more familiar from Fallout: New Vegas, following on from that final season one shot teasing the Strip.

title: The Anime That Broke the Filler Curse
description: Long before My Hero Academia, shonen adaptations like Naruto and Bleach just kept airing non-stop, which meant tons of padded-out filler arcs to keep pace with the manga. Studio Bones did things differently and released MHA in yearly seasonal chunks instead, which is a big part of why the pacing, animation and story all feel so much tighter than a lot of its shonen peers.

title: Star-Making Roles for the English Cast
description: For a chunk of the English dub cast, MHA was basically their big break. Justin Briner (Midoriya) and Clifford Chapin (Bakugo) both had this as a career-defining role, and Christopher Sabat took on All Might right around the same time he was already busy being the voice of Vegeta.

title: Magne's Casting Controversy
description: Magne, a trans woman in the League of Villains, is voiced by a cisgender man in both the original Japanese track and the English dub. It's one of those casting choices that still gets brought up whenever people talk about how anime handles trans representation.

title: Horikoshi Draws With a Comic in His Other Hand
description: Kohei Horikoshi is such a die-hard fan of American superhero comics that in one interview he flat out said he's often got a Japanese-translated Marvel or DC comic in one hand while he's actually drawing MHA pages with the other. He's also mentioned being especially fond of Spider-Man.

title: All Might Has a Bit of Goku in Him
description: All Might's mix of goofy, bumbling charm off-duty and total selflessness in a fight has often been pointed back to Dragon Ball's Goku as an influence. Horikoshi has openly cited Dragon Ball as one of his favorite series and a huge inspiration on how he built modern shonen heroes.

title: Why Horikoshi Kept MHA Shorter Than One Piece
description: Horikoshi has praised Eiichiro Oda's willingness to let characters speak their minds, something he leaned on heavily for Bakugo. But he's also said outright that he just doesn't have the stamina to write something on the scale of One Piece, which shaped his decision to keep MHA a more contained story rather than a decades-long saga.

title: Iron Might's Mecha Roots
description: The clunky, armored Iron Might suit that shows up later in the series isn't just a random support-item design. Horikoshi grew up drawing giant robots, and the suit is basically his love letter to old-school mecha anime like Mashin Hero Wataru from his childhood.

title: Eraserhead's Odd Hollywood Namesake
description: Aizawa's hero name comes straight from David Lynch's 1977 cult film Eraserhead, a surreal horror movie about the anxieties of parenthood that has genuinely nothing to do with quirks or teaching. Fans have gone back and forth for years on whether Aizawa's detached, deadpan personality was meant as a nod to the film's tone.

title: Gran Torino Is Named After the Clint Eastwood Movie
description: The retired, cane-wielding hero Gran Torino shares more than just a name with Clint Eastwood's 2008 film. Both are grumpy old war veterans who feel disconnected from the world around them but still can't help stepping in to protect people when it counts.

title: Plus Ultra Is a Hidden Signature
description: According to a breakdown from a professional MHA translator, the series' famous motto is basically Horikoshi signing his own name into the story. The 'koshi' in his surname uses the kanji for 'go beyond,' making Plus Ultra a sly bit of wordplay hidden in plain sight.

title: Plus Ultra Is an Actual National Motto
description: All Might didn't just invent his catchphrase out of thin air, the Latin phrase 'Plus Ultra' is the real-life motto of Spain, meaning 'further beyond.' It dates back centuries and shows up on the Spanish flag's coat of arms.

title: Best Jeanist's Name Is Literally a Denim Pun
description: Tsunagu Hakamada's hero name Best Jeanist is a pun lifted from a real denim enthusiast award, which lines up nicely with a Quirk that lets him manipulate fibers. Even his surname contains the kanji for hakama, a piece of traditional Japanese clothing.

title: Shigaraki's Name Is Basically a Funeral
description: Tomura Shigaraki's real name is built out of some pretty grim kanji, 'shi' for death, 'tomura' for mourning, and even the character for tree echoes the wooden grave markers used in Japanese cemeteries. His whole identity is basically spelled out before you even meet him.

title: Present Mic Might Be Named After a Real DJ
description: Present Mic's civilian name, Hizashi Yamada, is thought to be a small nod to Yamada Hisashi, a well-known Japanese radio DJ. It fits, considering Present Mic's whole hero persona is basically 'radio host with superpowers.'

title: Deku Started as an Insult and Became a Hero Name
description: Bakugo originally slapped the nickname 'Deku' on Midoriya as a jab, since it's Japanese slang for a useless wooden puppet and also happens to be a rough misreading of his actual name's kanji. It only became something positive after Uraraka pointed out it sounds a lot like 'dekiru,' meaning 'can do it,' and Midoriya decided to keep it as his hero name on his own terms.

title: Southeast Asia Got a Very Different Cut of the Show
description: Broadcasters in places like Indonesia and the Philippines heavily edited MHA for TV, cropping and zooming out swimsuit scenes and blurring Momo's costume to hide her cleavage. Violence got trimmed too, so a decent chunk of viewers in the region ended up watching a noticeably tamer version of the show.

title: A Christmas Episode Got Cut in the Middle East
description: Because Christmas isn't celebrated in Islam, broadcasters airing MHA in parts of the Middle East simply cut the Christmas-themed segments from episode 101 entirely. Mineta's more perverted moments were also toned down for the same broadcasters.

title: Toonami Quietly Un-Censored a Scene
description: A season three scene featuring Camie using her Quirk during the hero license exam originally aired more covered up than the manga intended. When Toonami later reran the episode, fans noticed the scene had actually been edited to show more skin than the original broadcast, undoing some of the earlier censorship.

title: Mirko's Big Injury Got Softened for TV
description: In the manga, Mirko loses her forearm and a leg in a brutal fight against a High-End Nomu, blood and all. Japan's stricter rules for early evening broadcast slots meant the anime toned the gore way down, cutting most of the blood so the injury reads as far less shocking on screen.

title: The Composer Who Never Shows Up Without His Dog
description: Series composer Yuki Hayashi is apparently something of a dog person, to the point where interviewers and photographers note he'll almost always have one of his dogs with him whenever he's being profiled or photographed.

title: Hayashi Composed the Whole Score Solo
description: On plenty of his other shows, like Haikyu!!, Yuki Hayashi split composing duties with fellow musician Asami Tachibana. For MHA he went it alone, cranking out 34 tracks for the first season and another 46 for the second entirely by himself.

title: One Piece Said Goodbye to MHA With a Teenage Doodle
description: When MHA's manga wrapped up, One Piece creator Eiichiro Oda marked the occasion by redrawing a piece of fan art a 15-year-old Horikoshi had actually mailed him 22 years earlier, long before Horikoshi was a professional artist. It's the same trick Oda pulled when Naruto and Dragon Ball ended, turning old fan submissions into farewell tributes.

title: Fans Honored Stan Lee Through Cellophane
description: When Stan Lee passed away, MHA fans online paid tribute by redrawing the classic 1963 Amazing Spider-Man #50 cover, but swapped Spider-Man's webbing for Sero's tape-based Cellophane Quirk. It's a fitting tribute given how openly MHA borrows from the Marvel aesthetic Lee helped build.

title: Motion-Captured by a Real Swordsman
description: Geralt's combat animations weren't just hand-keyed by animators. CD Projekt Red actually brought in a professional swordsman to perform the motion capture, and he found that a dance-like flow through each strike and parry felt far more natural than stiff, mechanical swings. That's exactly the fluid, almost balletic combat style that made it into the finished game.

title: A Map Bigger Than Skyrim
description: At launch, Witcher 3's open world was roughly 20% larger than Skyrim's map, and about 35 times the size of the world in The Witcher 2. That scale goes a long way toward explaining why the map ends up absolutely covered in little question marks waiting to be uncovered.

title: A Cut Fallout-Style Targeting System
description: At one point during development, the team experimented with a targeting system similar to Fallout's V.A.T.S, letting players pause combat and aim at specific body parts. It never made it into the final release, and honestly it's hard to picture the fast, fluid swordplay working any other way.

title: Over a Million Lines of Code
description: Building a world this size took some serious engineering. The finished game runs on more than a million lines of code, and a staggering 30,000 of those lines exist purely to handle dialogue.

title: The Author Stayed Out of It
description: Andrzej Sapkowski, the Polish novelist behind the books this whole series is built on, had no creative involvement in the direction CD Projekt Red took the story. All of the quests, characters, and choices players remember were shaped entirely by the studio's own writing team.

title: The Dev Team's Hidden Mountaintop Photo
description: Right at the peak of the tallest, most distant mountain visible from Toussaint, there's a framed photo of the actual development team propped on an easel between two pillars. There's no legitimate way to reach it during normal play, you need the game's debug free camera to teleport Geralt all the way up there.

title: Gwent Was Built in a Three-Day Sprint
description: Gwent almost never happened. Designers Damien Monnier and Rafal Jaki pitched a card game within the game, but studio head Adam Kiciński wasn't sold and only gave them three days to prove the idea could work. They pulled together a working demo over one long weekend, and it went on to become one of the most beloved parts of the entire game.

title: Gwent's Real-World Inspirations
description: When the Gwent team needed inspiration, they didn't turn to other fantasy card games. They borrowed ideas from the tabletop games War, Netrunner, and Condottiere to figure out how cards should move and interact on the board.

title: From Mini-Game to Standalone Hit
description: Gwent proved so popular that CD Projekt Red spun it off into its own free-to-play card game, and later into a single-player story campaign called Thronebreaker: The Witcher Tales. What started life as a way for Geralt to kill time between contracts ended up becoming a whole franchise on its own.

title: Gwent Finally Became a Physical Card Game
description: A full decade after Witcher 3 first launched, Gwent finally got turned into a real tabletop product, complete with over 400 physical cards, a playmat, and rules for both casual play and proper tournaments.

title: A New Single-Player Gwent Spin-off Is Coming
description: CD Projekt Red's in-house Gwent team has been quietly working on another standalone single-player card game, codenamed Project Golden Nekker. The studio has said it's meant to feel like its own thing rather than simply a repeat of the earlier Thronebreaker spin-off.

title: One Voice, Three Games (and a Movie)
description: Doug Cockle has voiced Geralt of Rivia in English across all three mainline Witcher games, sticking with the role for well over a decade. He's since confirmed he'll be reprising the part again for the animated film The Witcher: Sirens of the Deep.

title: Geralt's Voice Actor Calls the UK Home
description: Doug Cockle actually grew up in the US in a Marine Corps family before eventually settling in the UK with his wife back in 1999, where he still lives and works today. He holds both American and British citizenship.

title: Award Recognition for Geralt's Voice
description: Doug Cockle's performance as Geralt in Witcher 3 didn't go unnoticed by the industry. It earned him genuine critical acclaim along with multiple award nominations at major gaming awards ceremonies.

title: A Diablo Shout-Out in Fyresdal
description: Walk into the butcher's house in Fyresdal for the first time and he'll bellow 'Fresh Meat' the moment he spots you, the exact same line The Butcher shouts the first time you run into him in every Diablo game.

title: Legendary Swords with Borrowed Names
description: A couple of Witcher 3's silver swords are quiet nods to other classic RPGs. Azure Wrath echoes Azurewrath, the angelic blade wielded by the fallen angel Izual in the Diablo games, while a sword called Daystar borrows its name from the weapon guarded by a lich in Baldur's Gate's city of Amn.

title: The CDPR Logo Hiding in Toussaint
description: The Scarlet Cardinal Inn tucked away in Toussaint is a sly nod to CD Projekt Red's own company logo, hiding the studio's branding in plain sight as a tavern sign.

title: A Shawshank Redemption Nod
description: During the Hearts of Stone side quest The Drakenborg Redemption, a letter mentions a hidden stash and a promise to reunite with whoever left it there, a pretty clear wink at the setup from The Shawshank Redemption.

title: 'All Work and No Play' in Beauclair
description: A guard patrolling the streets of Beauclair mutters 'all work and no play' at Geralt, lifted straight from The Shining, right down to the delivery.

title: 'This is Skellige!'
description: Villagers and guards across Skellige will occasionally shout 'This is Skellige!' at the top of their lungs, an obvious riff on Leonidas' famous battle cry from 300.

title: A Monty Python Moment
entertainment: Monty Python and the Holy Grail
description: Tucked away somewhere in the game is a reference clearly lifted from Monty Python and the Holy Grail, which honestly fits given how much of Witcher 3's writing leans on dry, self-aware humour.

title: Red Hot Chili Peppers Get a Nod
description: Somewhere in the storybook world of the Land of a Thousand Fables, there's a bridge with an actual red pepper sitting underneath it, a cheeky little reference from developers who were clearly Red Hot Chili Peppers fans.

title: Smigole Serkis and His Precious Spoon
description: Somewhere in Blood and Wine there's a note written by a character called Smigole Serkis, mourning the loss of his beloved golden spoon. It's a two-for-one joke, poking fun at both Gollum's alter ego Smeagol and Andy Serkis, the actor who brought him to life.

title: Durden the Tailor
description: Check out a brawling tournament in Novigrad and you'll run into a character called Durden the Tailor, a fairly unsubtle nod to Tyler Durden from Fight Club.

title: A 127 Hours Reference in a Monster Cave
description: Deep inside one of the game's monster caves is a skeleton with its arm trapped under a fallen rock, a grim little homage to 127 Hours imagining what might have happened if the climber in that film never made it out.

title: Djenge Frett, Bounty Hunter
description: One of the bounty hunters Geralt runs into over in Skellige goes by the name Djenge Frett. Say it out loud a couple of times and it's not hard to hear the wink at Star Wars' Jango Fett.

title: A Godfather Line from Vesemir
description: Right near the start of the game, Vesemir describes Emperor Emhyr's summons as 'an offer one can't refuse,' borrowing one of The Godfather's most famous lines almost word for word.

title: Game of Thrones Easter Eggs Everywhere
description: Witcher 3 has more than one nod to Game of Thrones scattered through Skellige and Novigrad. A secondary quest even borrows its title, A Feast for Crows, straight from George R. R. Martin's fourth book in the series.

title: Why the Wild Hunt Wants Ciri
description: The Wild Hunt aren't the ghostly folklore riders that common folk on the Continent assume they are. They're actually elves from a different, dying world, crossing between dimensions in search of people carrying Elder Blood, like Ciri, because their own world is running out of options.

title: Born From a Cancelled MMO
description: Before Overwatch was even a concept, Blizzard spent years building a totally different game called Titan — a sprawling MMO where you'd clock into a day job and then run secret-agent missions at night. It just never came together, but a chunk of the character art and environments got recycled straight into Overwatch once Titan got the axe.

title: 48 Heroes Pitched in One Morning
description: After Titan died, the leftover dev team (Team 4) had six weeks to come up with something new. On one particular morning everyone on the team had to pitch a hero idea, and by lunch they'd racked up 48 concepts — including a Russian woman riding a bear and dual-wielding AK-47s, whose ultimate had the bear pull out guns too. That one didn't make the cut, somehow.

title: Genji and Hanzo Were One Hero
description: Early on, Genji and Hanzo weren't two brothers at all — they were a single cyborg ninja hero with a big grab-bag of tricks. Devs realised that was way too much character crammed into one kit, so they split it into two, and honestly the brother rivalry angle works a lot better than one guy trying to do everything.

title: D.Va's Pre-Mech Career
description: Before she was piloting a mech for MEKA, Hana Song was a professional StarCraft player. It's a nice bit of world-building that ties the near-future setting back to Blizzard's other games without spelling it out — you'd only catch it if you actually read into her backstory.

title: Torbjörn's Ultimate Is a WoW Callback
description: Torbjörn's ultimate ability is called Molten Core, which is a direct nod to one of the most famous raid dungeons in World of Warcraft. Small detail, but it's the kind of thing that makes long-time Blizzard fans grin when they finally clock it.

title: The Arcade in Hanamura
description: Wander into the arcade on the Hanamura map and you'll spot cabinets referencing both StarCraft and Heroes of the Storm sitting right next to each other. Blizzard loves cross-pollinating its own universe, and this little corner is basically a shrine to it.

title: A Trademark Beat Blizzard to the Name
description: Years before Blizzard's game existed, a company called Innovis Labs actually filed a trademark for the name 'Overwatch' back in 2013 — for a paintball app, of all things. Not exactly the same energy as the hero shooter, but the name was technically spoken for first.

title: Widowmaker Used to Be Happily Married
description: It's easy to forget, but Widowmaker wasn't always the ice-cold assassin she is now. As Amélie Lacroix, she was married to Overwatch agent Gérard Lacroix — and it was through him that Talon got their hands on her and rewired her into the person we play today.

title: Why Mercy Hates Violence
description: Mercy comes across as the group's gentle healer, but her backstory isn't quite that soft — her parents were killed in combat, which is where her deep discomfort with Overwatch's more violent methods actually comes from. She helps because she believes it's the best way to limit the damage, not because she's naive to it.

title: Sigma's Research Broke His Own Mind
description: Sigma was obsessed with cracking the science behind gravity and black holes, and that obsession is literally what fractured his sanity. He comes off eccentric and a bit unsettling in-game, but the lore makes clear he's not malicious — just a genius who got too close to something he couldn't fully control.

title: Sombra Is Chasing a Hidden Conspiracy
description: There's a running thread in Overwatch lore about a conspiracy that isn't Overwatch or Talon — something bigger tying nearly every character together. Sombra's the only one actively digging into it, and her research suggests basically the entire cast has some kind of connection to it, even if most players never notice.

title: Reinhardt's Surprisingly Close Tie
description: Most heroes are two or three steps removed from Sombra's mystery conspiracy, but Reinhardt is unusually close to it — directly linked to someone who's directly linked to it. Nobody's said out loud who that connection actually is yet, which makes it one of the more intriguing loose threads in the whole story.

title: Pharah Grew Up Idolizing Overwatch
description: Long before she suited up as Pharah, Fareeha Amari was a kid who was completely obsessed with Overwatch and everything it stood for. It makes her eventual path into the organization feel less like a coincidence and more like something she was working toward her whole life.

title: Murlocs Snuck Into Overwatch
description: Blizzard couldn't resist bringing their favorite little WoW menace along for the ride. There's a giant murloc slurping a bowl of ramen in Hanamura, murloc plushies up for grabs in the arcade, and murloc graffiti tucked away at Temple of Anubis. None of it means anything, it's just Blizzard being Blizzard.

title: A Dark Souls Bonfire in Eichenwalde
description: Next to the defenders' second spawn on Eichenwalde, you'll find a sword jammed into a bonfire — a straight-up nod to the resting spots in Dark Souls. They even put a big health pack right beside it, which is a nice touch if you know what you're looking at.

title: Route 66's Payload Is Actually a Rescue
description: On Route 66, the attacking team is technically pushing stolen cargo for the Deadlock Gang — except the 'cargo' was meant to be Echo before Cassidy stepped in and rescued her. So functionally, you spend the whole match pushing an empty crate while the actual point of the heist already got resolved off-screen.

title: Numbani's Cargo Used to Be a Legendary Gauntlet
description: Numbani's payload didn't always go to a museum for mystery cargo — it used to be the Doomfist gauntlet itself, headed to an exhibit dedicated to the three men who'd worn it over the years. The cargo got swapped out later, likely because the gauntlet ended up back in the hands of the third Doomfist, Akande Ogundimu.

title: Hollywood's Cargo Is a HAL 9000 Pun
description: The 'cargo' on Hollywood isn't cargo at all — it's an Omnic named HAL-Fred Glitchbot who's being escorted through the studio lot while an anti-Omnic group tries to take him out. The name's a little wink at classic sci-fi that's easy to miss if you're too busy fighting over the payload.

title: Route 66's Warehouse Ships to Other Maps
description: Look closely at the crates in the Route 66 warehouse and you'll spot they're addressed to businesses from completely different maps — Lumérico in Dorado, Rikimaru in Hanamura, Kofi Aromo's café in Numbani. It's a small detail that makes the world feel a lot more connected than any single match lets on.

title: The IT Crowd Hidden in a Grillmaster Skin
description: Take a close look at the barcode on Soldier: 76's Biotic Field when he's wearing the Grillmaster skin and you'll find the number 0118 999 881 999 119 7253 — the fake 'easy to remember' emergency number from The IT Crowd. Cheeky pick given the item's whole job is healing people.

title: Sombra's Spray Hides a Reference Inside a Reference
description: Sombra's 'Deaf-Mute' spray nods to the Laughing Man from Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex — and that character's own catchphrase is itself lifted from The Catcher in the Rye. It's a reference wrapped inside another reference, which feels very on-brand for a hacker character.

title: Sojourn's Spray Recreates a Predator Moment
description: One of Sojourn's sprays, 'Old Soldiers,' is a shot-for-shot recreation of that famous arm-wrestling handshake between Dutch and Dillon in Predator. If you've seen the movie, it's instantly recognizable — if you haven't, it just looks like a really intense high-five.

title: Torbjörn Is Secretly the Swedish Chef
description: Torbjörn has a spray called 'Chef' that's basically him doing a dead-on impression of the Swedish Chef from The Muppets — same energy, same chaotic kitchen vibes, just with a lot more welding.

title: Genji Quotes The Princess Bride
description: Genji has a voice line, 'You seem nice, I hate to kill you,' that's a pretty direct lift from Inigo Montoya's duel with the Dread Pirate Roberts in The Princess Bride. It fits Genji's whole honorable-swordsman thing a bit too perfectly to be a coincidence.

title: The Horse Testicles Actually React to Weather
description: Somebody at Rockstar genuinely had this as part of their job. Ride a male horse out into the snowy mountains and, if you look closely enough, you'll notice things shrink up in the cold and settle back down once you're somewhere warmer. It got so much attention before launch that the studio ended up confirming it themselves rather than letting fans keep guessing.

title: $725 Million Before the First Week Was Even Over
description: Launch weekend for RDR2 wasn't just good, it was one of the biggest openings any piece of entertainment has ever had. Rockstar reported around $725 million in sales in just the first three days, putting it up there with blockbuster movie openings rather than typical game launches.

title: Every Rockstar Studio Worked on This One Game
description: Rather than splitting work across separate teams, Rockstar pulled all of its studios worldwide together into one combined production for RDR2. That's over 2,000 people, from the motion capture performers right through to the environment artists, all pointed at the same game for years.

title: A Script Longer Than Most Novels
description: A typical film script runs somewhere around 120 pages. RDR2's story missions and side content reportedly ran past 2,000 pages of script, and that figure doesn't even include the roughly eighty extra pages written just so background pedestrians would have something to mutter as you walk by.

title: Arthur Morgan Didn't Exist Yet When RDR1 Came Out
description: Go back and play the first game and you won't hear Arthur's name mentioned anywhere. Rockstar never had a sequel planned when RDR1 released, so one of the most loved characters in gaming simply hadn't been written yet at that point.

title: Uncle's Actor Didn't Live to See the Game Finished
description: There's a bittersweet story behind all the 'Uncle has lumbago' jokes. John O'Creagh, who performed and voiced Uncle, passed away from a blood clot complication partway through the game's production. Rockstar removed most of his recorded lines out of respect, though the unused files still sit in the game's data. The one performance of his that made it into the finished game is his singing during the celebration scene at Beecher's Hope.

title: Crouch-Running Was the Hardest Part of the Whole Shoot
description: Roger Clark, who did the motion capture and voice for Arthur, has said the toughest physical challenge of the entire production wasn't a big emotional scene, it was crouch-running. He spent something like three days repeating crouch-walks and crouch-runs with different weapons in hand, and joked afterwards that his thighs were wrecked for days.

title: Arthur's Illness Was Inspired by a Real Family Story
description: Arthur's slow decline from tuberculosis wasn't just chosen for dramatic effect. Co-founder Dan Houser has since said it was personal to him, his own grandfather contracted tuberculosis before antibiotics existed, not long after Dan's father was born, and that piece of family history shaped how Arthur's story was written to end.

title: The Phantom Train of Lemoyne
description: Ride near the train tracks in northern Lemoyne around 3am and your horse might start acting spooked for no obvious reason. Stick around and a ghostly train comes barrelling down the line before fading away. It's never explained in-game, but a fair few players reckon it's a wink towards the phantom train boss fight from Final Fantasy VI.

title: There's a UFO Hiding Near Mount Shann
description: This one takes a bit of legwork to trigger. Find the small shack north of Emerald Station in New Hanover and read the note left inside, then climb Mount Shann and track down an odd rock circle near the summit. Head back to that same shack once night falls and you'll see a green glow drifting through the sky above it.

title: A Giant Skeleton on Mount Shann
description: Rockstar can never resist a Sasquatch nod, and RDR2 hides one on Mount Shann, north of Strawberry. Climb high enough and you'll find an enormous skeleton lodged in the rock. The game never says what it is outright, but most players are fairly certain it's meant to be Bigfoot.

title: The Man in the Game Files Called COUGAR_MAN
description: Out in the wilderness sits a corpse with a strange, almost feline curl to his lip. Dig through the game's internal files and he's actually labelled COUGAR_MAN, which has led people to tie him back to an old glitch from the original Red Dead Redemption where a human character model somehow ended up with a cougar's attributes.

title: A Church Built for Someone Much Smaller Than Arthur
description: Deep in the swamps of Bayou Nwa, past the gators and the outlaws trying to kill you, there's a genuinely tiny little church. Arthur can only just fit through the doorway, and the pews inside look like they were built for someone a fraction of his size.

title: The Undead Nightmare Mask Is Hiding in Plain Sight
