description: Take a proper look behind the counter at the Saint Denis general store and you'll spot the Undead Mask from the first game's zombie-themed Undead Nightmare expansion sitting on a shelf. It's purely a display piece this time around though, you can't pick it up or wear it.

title: Something Is Locked Inside That Outhouse
description: Near Braithwaite Manor there's a chained-shut outhouse that's easy to walk straight past. Get close enough and you'll hear a woman inside muttering gibberish to herself. Switch to first-person and peer through the gaps and she might just lunge at you. The game never tells you what, exactly, she is.

title: The Night Folk of Bluewater Marsh
description: Head into Bluewater Marsh after dark and you might come across a crying woman, or grim little scenes of bodies strung up in the trees. Get too close to either and the Night Folk will crawl out of hiding to come after you. Anyone who played the original game's Undead Nightmare DLC will recognise the vibe instantly.

title: A Secret That Went Unnoticed for Seven Years
description: Years after release, players including Pariah87 and goldenplaysterraria stumbled on a spider-web symbol carved into a telegraph pole that nobody had ever documented before. It went viral in the community all over again, and even with plenty of digging, nobody has managed to fully explain what it's actually referencing.

title: Dutch's Boys Are Named for Real Outlaw Gangs
description: The way the gang gets talked about in-game echoes two very real crews from the era: Butch Cassidy's Wild Bunch and the Dalton Gang, both of whom actually rode through the American West around the same period the game is set in.

title: Black Belle Is Built From Two Real Outlaw Women
description: The character Black Belle borrows from two very different real-life figures at once, Belle Starr, the outlaw known as the 'Bandit Queen', and Annie Oakley, the famous sharpshooter. Rockstar seems to have blended traits from both into the one fictional character.

title: Billy Midnight Nods to the Man Who Shot Jesse James
description: The name Billy Midnight is a reference to Robert Ford, the real outlaw remembered for shooting his own gang leader Jesse James in the back. He's one of several characters scattered through the game built around real names from Wild West history.

title: Desirée LaFlamme Is a Reference to Two Very Different Things
description: The barrel-riding stunt performer Desirée LaFlamme nods to two unrelated sources at once, Annie Edson Taylor, the real woman who survived going over Niagara Falls in a barrel in 1901, and Tauriel from The Hobbit: The Desolation of Smaug.

title: The Game That Started as 'Cave Game'
description: Before it had its iconic name, Minecraft was a scrappy little project Notch was calling Cave Game while he tinkered with it in his spare time. He was openly borrowing ideas from Dwarf Fortress, Infiniminer and even RollerCoaster Tycoon, mashing them together into something nobody had quite seen before. Funny to think the biggest game on the planet started life sounding like a budget dungeon crawler.

title: Built in Under a Week
description: Notch didn't spend years agonising over the first version of Minecraft, he banged out the alpha in just six days back in May 2009. It was barebones compared to what we play now, but the core idea of punching blocks and building whatever you wanted was already there, ready to snowball into a global obsession.

title: The $2.5 Billion Tweet
description: Notch selling Minecraft to Microsoft wasn't some long boardroom saga, by his own account it kicked off after he vented his frustration with the community in a single tweet in June 2014. A few months later Microsoft had bought Mojang for $2.5 billion, and Notch, along with co-founders Carl Manneh and Jakob Porser, walked away from the company entirely.

title: Wiping Notch Off the Title Screen
description: Long after the sale, Mojang quietly stripped out some of the splash text jokes that used to flash across the main menu, including 'Made by Notch!', 'The Work of Notch!' and a cheeky '110813!' referencing his old wedding date. He's still credited in the closing credits, but that little nod on the title screen is gone for good.

title: The Best-Selling Game on the Planet
description: Somewhere around 2023 Minecraft crossed the 300 million copies sold mark, officially making it the best-selling video game ever recorded, according to Guinness World Records. By 2025 that number had climbed past 350 million, and there's still no real sign of it slowing down more than a decade and a half after launch.

title: Bigger Than Earth Itself
description: A default Minecraft world stretches out to a 60,000km wide square, which sounds abstract until you realise that's several times larger than the entire surface area of Earth. Nobody is ever walking the whole thing, but it's a wild bit of trivia to drop on someone who thinks they've 'explored everything' in their save file.

title: The Glitch at the Edge of the World
description: Long before world borders were a thing, players who walked far enough from spawn in older versions would hit the Far Lands, a stretch of terrain around 12.5 million blocks out where the game's math simply broke down into towering, glitched cliffs. It took a YouTuber a legitimate ten-day walk in 2020 just to reach it, since the spot got patched out of normal generation years earlier.

title: One Guy Voices Almost Everything
description: Turns out the huge cast of grunting, roaring, sniffing mobs you hear wandering around your world mostly comes down to one person. Mojang's audio director Samuel Aberg does the villagers, the sniffers, the piglins and plenty more himself, layering and pitching his own voice to get that range of sounds, with only a few effects (like the arrow thud, which is actually a rattling chair) coming from elsewhere.

title: A Library Built to Dodge Censorship
description: Reporters Without Borders realised that in countries where the free press gets blocked, Minecraft servers often still slip through the firewall. So they built The Uncensored Library, a genuinely massive structure made from over 12.5 million blocks, packed with banned articles and books from places like Russia, Egypt and Belarus, giving young people a sneaky way to read what their governments don't want them to see.

title: NASA Sends Players to the Moon
description: NASA has actually partnered with Minecraft Education on more than one occasion, first getting kids to plan and launch rockets in an Artemis-themed set of worlds, then building out interactive modules based on real James Webb Space Telescope imagery so students can piece together star formation and galaxy types for themselves. It's one of the more surprising ways a block-building game has ended up doubling as a genuine STEM classroom tool.

title: Notch Doesn't Have a Brother
description: Herobrine has to be the most famous thing in Minecraft that was never actually in Minecraft. The whole legend traces back to a 2010 forum post claiming a white-eyed figure was haunting someone's world, supposedly the ghost of Notch's dead brother. Notch has flat out said he doesn't have one, but the myth took on a life of its own anyway and is still one of the game's most enduring urban legends.

title: Removed Herobrine (Again)
description: Mojang leaned into the Herobrine hysteria so hard that they've written 'Removed Herobrine' into the changelog of pretty much every major update since 2012, despite the character never once existing in the game's code. It's become a running joke between the developers and the community, a wink to a myth that refuses to die.

title: The Enderman's Creepy Cousin
description: That unsettling stillness the Enderman has, staring you down before it snaps into a rage, wasn't an accident. Notch has acknowledged the mob's look and behaviour were shaped by Slenderman, the tall, faceless internet legend that was already spreading through horror forums when the Enderman was designed for the game's Adventure Update.

title: The Ghast's Secret Voice Actor
description: Those unnerving Ghast screeches drifting through the Nether aren't some digitally engineered monster sound, they're a real cat. Composer C418 apparently caught his own cat's startled meow on a recording session, and rather than replace it, that panicked yowl got worked straight into the Ghast's audio and has stayed there ever since.

title: A Poem the Company Never Owned
description: The End Poem, that dreamy nine-minute scroll of text you get after beating the Ender Dragon, was written by novelist Julian Gough as a favour to his friend Notch. He never actually signed the contract handing the rights over to Mojang, and in 2022, after a falling out with the company, he released the whole poem into the public domain rather than let Microsoft claim it.

title: Flip a Mob Upside Down
description: Grab a name tag, scribble 'Dinnerbone' or 'Grumm' onto it, and slap it on almost any mob in the game, and it'll flop upside down for the rest of its life. It's a tribute to Mojang's technical director Nathan 'Dinnerbone' Adams, whose own online avatar has always been rendered flipped, and the joke stuck so well it's become a permanent feature rather than a bug.

title: Rainbow Sheep on Command
description: Naming a sheep 'jeb_' with a name tag turns its wool into a slow, glitchy cycle through every dye colour in the game, like a tiny woolly disco ball wandering your farm. It's a little tip of the hat to Mojang's Jens 'Jeb' Bergensten, though shearing one still just gives you the sheep's original, boring colour of wool.

title: A Rabbit Named After a Real Pet
description: Name a rabbit 'Toast' and it swaps to a unique brown and white skin that has nothing to do with breakfast. It's actually a quiet memorial to a real rabbit that went missing from its owner, a Minecraft forum user, back when the mob was being added, and Mojang decided to bake the tribute permanently into the game.

title: Here's Johnny
description: Rename a Vindicator 'Johnny' and it stops caring about teams entirely, turning hostile toward every other mob in the game except Ghasts and fellow illagers. It's a direct nod to Jack Nicholson's iconic 'Here's Johnny!' moment from The Shining, and once that name tag goes on there's no calming him back down.

title: The Cake Is (Still) a Lie
description: Bake your very first cake in Minecraft and the achievement you unlock is simply called 'The Lie', a cheeky little wink at Portal's endlessly quotable line about the cake being a lie. It's easy to miss if you're not already in on the joke, but once you know it's there you can't unsee it every time you go for that early-game achievement.

title: Wings Borrowed From a Plumber
description: The Elytra, Minecraft's glider wings that let you swan-dive off mountains and soar across the map, plays almost identically to the Wing Cap power-up from Super Mario 64. It's not officially billed as a crossover, but the gliding feel is close enough that plenty of long-time Mario fans clocked the resemblance the moment the update dropped.

title: Klingon, Pirate Speak and LOLCat
description: Dig into the language settings and Minecraft isn't just offering the usual list of real-world languages, you can switch your whole interface over to Pirate Speak, Shakespearean English, or even Klingon if you're feeling committed. It's a small detail that says a lot about how Notch wanted the game to feel silly and welcoming rather than sterile.

title: A Cat's Meow Gave Endermen Their Voice
description: It's not just the Ghast, that eerie Enderman noise you hear right before it teleports and lunges at you traces back to the same batch of cat recordings the developers used for other mobs. Layer and pitch-shift a startled cat enough times and apparently you get one of the most feared sounds in the entire game.

title: Second Only to Tetris
description: As huge as Minecraft's sales numbers are, it still isn't technically the single best-selling game of all time once you count Tetris, which has racked up over 520 million units across its many different versions since the 1980s. Minecraft holds the record for best-selling single title from one continuous release, which is its own remarkable feat given it's had virtually no sequels or reboots to pad the numbers.

title: The 18-Month Miracle
description: Obsidian only had about a year and a half to build the entire game, which is nuts when you think most RPGs of that size take three or four years minimum. Director Josh Sawyer has said a couple of those months were eaten up just on early planning, so the actual build time was even tighter. It's honestly a big part of why the game shipped a little rough around the edges, but also why the writing feels so sharp and focused.

title: One Point Short of a Fortune
description: Bethesda's contract with Obsidian included a big bonus if the game hit a certain Metacritic score. New Vegas came in one single point below that target, which meant Obsidian lost out on a large chunk of the payout despite the game becoming a fan favourite. It's one of those stories that gets brought up constantly whenever people talk about how brutal review-score bonus clauses can be for developers.

title: Born From a Cancelled Game
description: Long before New Vegas existed, Black Isle was working on a game called Van Buren that got cancelled. A surprising amount of that scrapped project made it into New Vegas anyway, most notably Caesar's Legion, which was originally written for Van Buren. Even the Big Empty from Old World Blues traces back to an early Van Buren location idea.

title: Ulysses Almost Rode With You
description: Ulysses, the mysterious antagonist from the Lonesome Road DLC, was originally written to be a companion you could recruit in the base game. He got cut for time, but the personality stuck around and shaped who he became later. If he'd made it in as planned, he'd have been the only companion who actually sympathised with Caesar's Legion while still distrusting the NCR, which would have made for some interesting party banter.

title: Romance Options Were Cut Early
description: There were plans at one point for actual romance mechanics between the player and companions, but the idea got dropped early in development. You can still see a trace of it in the companion roster though, since the four human companions work out to two men and two women, with one of each being gay, so the game was clearly built with the option in mind before it was scrapped.

title: Ron Perlman's Long Run as the Narrator
description: Ron Perlman opens New Vegas the same way he's opened every mainline Fallout game since the 1997 original, with that instantly recognisable 'war never changes' narration. By this point it's basically the voice of the whole franchise, and it's wild to think Bethesda kept bringing him back across totally different developers and console generations.

title: Matthew Perry Plays the Guy Who Shoots You
description: The smooth-talking gangster Benny, the man responsible for putting a bullet in the Courier's head at the start of the game, is voiced by Matthew Perry. It's a genuinely different kind of role for him compared to the sitcom work he was best known for, and he leans into the sleazy charm really well.

title: Mr. Las Vegas Plays Mr. New Vegas
description: Casting Wayne Newton as the radio host Mr. New Vegas is one of those decisions that just makes too much sense. Newton had been performing in actual Las Vegas for decades and was practically synonymous with the city, so having him play the smooth-voiced DJ of the Mojave's own radio station was a perfect bit of stunt casting that also happened to work brilliantly.

title: Worf Voices the Super Mutant
description: Michael Dorn, best known for playing Worf, returns as the super mutant Marcus, a character he'd already voiced back in Fallout 2. It's a nice bit of continuity for long-time fans, bringing back the same actor for a character who'd been off-screen since the second game in the series.

title: A Country Legend Plays a War-Weary Soldier
description: Kris Kristofferson, the country singer and actor from the Blade films, voices Chief Hanlon, the tired old NCR soldier who's grown disillusioned with the war for Hoover Dam. His weathered, gravelly delivery fits the character's exhaustion perfectly, which is probably exactly why he was cast.

title: Dave Foley Is the Happiest AI in the Wasteland
description: The relentlessly cheerful, slightly unsettling Yes Man is voiced by Dave Foley of Kids in the Hall and NewsRadio fame. His upbeat, chipper tone is exactly what makes Yes Man so quietly creepy, since he's happy to help you no matter which ending you're steering the Mojave toward.

title: No Elvis Songs, Just Elvis Everything Else
description: Obsidian clearly wanted Elvis all over this game, but they couldn't afford the licensing to actually use his music. Instead you get quest names that nod to his songs and films without ever playing them, like Nothin' But a Hound Dog, Return to Sender, and Viva Las Vegas. It's a clever workaround for a budget problem that ended up becoming its own little easter egg trail for fans who know their Elvis catalogue.

title: The Tops' House Band Is a Rat Pack Tribute
description: The performers at the Aces theater in the Tops, led by Tommy Torini, are called the Rad Pack Revue, a direct play on the real-world Rat Pack of Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin, Sammy Davis Jr., and friends. It goes a step further too, since actual Sinatra and Martin recordings show up on the in-game radio, tying the joke together nicely.

title: A Deep Cut Wrestling Reference
description: During the G.I. Blues quest you can find three men camped out named Roy, Wayne, and Farris. Put those together and you get Roy Wayne Farris, the real name of 80s wrestling star The Honky Tonk Man. It's such an obscure reference that even people who've played the game dozens of times tend to miss it completely.

title: Stripe the Mini Deathclaw Is a Gremlins Nod
description: In Old World Blues there's a tiny but surprisingly tough deathclaw called Stripe, and yes, that's a direct reference to the gremlin of the same name from the 1984 film. Get too close to him and he'll actually flee toward a fountain, mirroring the exact spot where the movie's Stripe meets his end.

title: White Bird Drops an Internet Meme
description: During Honest Hearts, the tribal character White Bird can randomly blurt out the line 'take drugs, kill a bear,' which sounds completely out of place coming from him. It's actually a nod to an old advice animal meme format that was floating around online at the time, and the contrast between his character and the line is exactly what makes it land.

title: A Fridge Straight Out of Indiana Jones
entertainment: Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull
description: If you're playing with the Wild Wasteland trait switched on, head southeast of Goodsprings early in the game and you'll find a skeleton inside a blown-out refrigerator. It's a direct callback to the moment in the fourth Indiana Jones film where he survives a nuclear blast by hiding inside a lead-lined fridge, except in the wasteland, that plan clearly didn't work out so well.

title: The Director Made His Own Unofficial Patch
description: Game director Josh Sawyer built his own personal mod, unofficially nicknamed JSawyer, that rebalances a lot of systems and fixes issues he felt never got resolved before launch. It's essentially his own director's cut of the game, made purely out of passion rather than any studio mandate, and fans still use it today when they want the experience closer to his original vision.

title: The Khans Are Part Biker Gang, Part Great Plains Tribe
description: The Great Khans, the drug-running faction you find holed up in Red Rock Canyon, were designed as a blend of real motorcycle gang culture and Great Plains Native American history, drawing loosely on groups like the Kansa, Osage, and Cheyenne alongside the aesthetic of clubs like the Mongols MC. It's a strange combination on paper, but it gives them a distinct identity compared to every other faction in the Mojave.

title: The Gambler Hides in the Caravan Minigame
description: The Caravan card game challenges Know When to Fold 'Em and Know When to Hold 'Em are lifted straight from the lyrics of Kenny Rogers' classic song The Gambler. It's a small touch, but it fits the whole Vegas-casino vibe of the game so well that it almost feels like it should have always been there.

title: A Perk Named After a 1950s Doo-Wop Hit
description: The Mister Sandman perk, which lets you kill sleeping targets silently, takes its name from the 1954 song of the same name by The Chordettes. Given how much of the game's soundtrack and quest naming leans on 50s and 60s music, it fits right in with everything else going on around it.

title: Children Are Almost Nowhere to Be Found
description: There's a noticeable lack of child characters wandering around the Mojave. Early on the team apparently planned to bring back Fallout 3's Child at Heart perk, but because so few kids ended up in the final game, the perk was left in as unused code that never actually gets triggered by anything.

title: Danny Trejo Plays the Wasteland's Best Mechanic
description: Raul Tejada, the ghoul companion and gifted mechanic you can rescue from Black Mountain, is voiced by Danny Trejo. It's a fun bit of casting when you consider Trejo had already built a career playing tough, world-weary characters, and Raul, an old gunslinger who's outlived pretty much everyone he ever cared about, fits that mould nicely.

title: Prost Bar
description: Tucked away on the edge of Boston Common, just past Swan's Pond, there's a rundown little watering hole called Prost Bar - and it's basically a love letter to Cheers. Prost is German for 'cheers', and the layout mirrors the show's set almost beat for beat. Two skeletons sit at the end of the bar in the exact spots where Cliff and Norm always parked themselves, and if you duck into the back office you'll find a stash of baseball grenades, a nod to Sam Malone's playing days with the Red Sox.

title: World of Refreshment
description: Nuka-World's World of Refreshment ride is Fallout's take on the chocolate river from Willy Wonka. Guests used to sail through it in boats, just like in Roald Dahl's book, and there's even a terminal entry encouraging visitors to drink straight from the river - basically the opposite advice Wonka gave his guests. These days it's just full of nukalurks and murky Nuka-Quantum instead of chocolate, so maybe don't take a sip.

title: Knight-Captain Cade's Medical Emergency
description: The Prydwen's chief medic, Knight-Captain Cade, has a line that Star Trek fans will clock instantly. Greet him for a check-up and there's a chance he'll say 'Please state the nature of your medical emergency' - the exact stock phrase used by the Doctor in Star Trek: Voyager. It's an especially neat touch since Cade is voiced by Dwight Schultz, who actually appeared in Voyager as Lieutenant Barclay.

title: MacCready's Library Line
description: Bring MacCready along to the Boston Public Library and he'll drop a line straight out of Ghostbusters. Walking into the ransacked main hall, he mutters something like 'no human being would possibly pile books this way' - a direct riff on Bill Murray's line during the Ghostbusters' library scene. Small moment, but it lands if you know the movie.

title: The Bradburton Bonfire
description: Out past Nuka-World in the town of Bradburton, there's a burned-out house with a sword stuck in a pile of glowing embers by the front door. Light it and stimpaks pop out; take the sword and you get three more. It's a straight-up Dark Souls reference, right down to acting like a little healing checkpoint.

title: Nick Valentine Quotes The Raven
description: When the Prydwen makes its dramatic entrance over the Commonwealth, Nick Valentine will recite 'Deep into that darkness peering, long I stood there, wondering, fearing...' if he's travelling with you - a line lifted straight from Edgar Allan Poe's The Raven. Good bit of atmosphere for a giant airship showing up out of nowhere.

title: The Cask of Amontillado at the Castle
description: Down in the tunnels beneath the Castle, you'll find General McGann's body next to a crate of wine and, just across the way, a skeleton sealed inside a bricked-up wall. It's a pretty clear nod to Poe's The Cask of Amontillado, and the wine even matches - it's Amontillado.

title: Companions Quote Monty Python
entertainment: Monty Python and the Holy Grail
description: Fallout 4 sneaks in a good three Monty Python and the Holy Grail references through your companions. Cait can bring up the Black Knight fight ('what are you gonna do, leak oil all over me?'), Codsworth has his own Black Knight line ('Tis but a scratch!'), and Deacon has a whole bit about taunting turrets that mirrors the French Knight scene. All of it can slip by completely unnoticed if you're not paying attention to companion chatter.

title: Bullet In The Knee
description: Get a raider low on health and there's a decent chance they'll scream something about a bullet in the knee - a cheeky flip on Skyrim's infamous 'arrow to the knee' guard line. Bethesda clearly wasn't going to let that meme go unreferenced.

title: Nirnroot's Fallout Cousin
description: Up in Senior Scribe Neriah's lab on the Prydwen, there's a tray of experimental plants described as growing near rivers. Sound familiar? It's basically Fallout's version of Skyrim's nirnroot, minus the annoying chime. Thankfully you can harvest it without hunting down that sound for twenty minutes.

title: Pickman Gallery & Kingsport Lighthouse
description: H.P. Lovecraft fans have plenty to chew on in the Commonwealth. Pickman Gallery and its unsettling artist owner are a nod to Lovecraft's short story Pickman's Model, while the Kingsport Lighthouse borrows its name from Lovecraft's fictional seaside town, seen in stories like The Terrible Old Man. Dunwich Borers piles on even more of the same eldritch dread.

title: Tears In Rain On The Mass Fusion Rooftop
description: Climb up to the roof of the Mass Fusion Containment Shed and you'll find a raider and a dead synth arranged in a way that mirrors the 'tears in rain' finale of Blade Runner. It's easy to miss since you need to clamber up some pipes and an air conditioning unit to spot it, but it's a genuinely moody little scene once you're up there.

title: Takahashi's Blade Runner Line
description: Diamond City's noodle vendor Takahashi has exactly one line of dialogue, and it's lifted word for word, broken grammar included, from Blade Runner's noodle bar scene. Blink and you'll miss it, but it's one of several Blade Runner nods scattered around the game.

title: Red Menace On The Pip-Boy
description: Buried in holotapes across the Commonwealth is a playable Pip-Boy game called Red Menace, which is basically Bethesda's tribute to the original Donkey Kong. It's easy to overlook since you have to actually find and load the holotape yourself, but it's a proper little arcade throwback hiding in your wrist computer.

title: Swan's Tragic Origin
description: That terrifying Super Mutant Behemoth guarding the pond in Boston Common used to be a man named Edward Swann, a convict who volunteered for prisoner reduction tests and ended up dosed with FEV. His journal entries chart the whole grim decline, starting with a boost to strength and intelligence, then a slow collapse into the mindless rage monster you eventually fight.

title: Vault 95's Rehab Experiment
description: Vault 95 was pitched to its residents as a rehab facility for chem addicts, but Vault-Tec quietly stashed a huge cache of drugs inside as part of the experiment. Once people found it, things fell apart fast - staff were killed and the vault dwellers overdosed in waves. You can still find their bodies slumped around the vault today, chems scattered nearby.

title: Vault 114's Unqualified Overseer
description: Vault 114 was meant to be a haven for the Commonwealth's wealthiest, but the overseer picked to run it was a homeless man with no leadership experience and some fairly severe schizophrenic tendencies, nicknamed Soupcan Harry. It was less a shelter and more a study in what happens when the privileged get put under a lunatic's charge, and the body count in there tells you how that went.

title: Deacon's Dark Past
description: Deacon's laid-back charm hides a genuinely dark past. He used to run with a synth-hating gang called the University Point Deathclaws, until the group killed a synth who turned out to be a real human. Disgusted, Deacon walked away, settled down and got married, only for his old gang to track him down and kill his wife, revealing in the process that she'd been a synth the whole time. It's why he ended up working for the Railroad.

title: Curie And The Synth Family Tree
description: Curie starts life as a Mr. Handy-style robot before transferring her mind into a synth body so she can properly research what it means to be human. It's a lovely arc on its own, but there's a weirder wrinkle buried in the game's lore: every generation 3 synth, Curie included, is built from genetic material derived from your character's son, Shaun.

title: The Ford Nucleon Wrecks
description: Those rusted-out, exploding cars scattered across the Commonwealth aren't random Bethesda design - they're modeled on the Ford Nucleon, a real 1950s concept car that would have run on a small nuclear reactor. It fits the franchise's whole retro-futuristic vibe a little too perfectly.

title: Codsworth's Secret Name List
description: Codsworth can recognise and say almost a thousand pre-recorded player names, which is already a lot of work for a video game companion. On top of the published list floating around online, the developers quietly snuck in a handful of extra names players only discovered through trial, error, and a lot of save-scumming.

title: Seven Years In The Making
description: Fallout 4's first piece of concept art was made in 2009, about a week after Fallout 3's final DLC wrapped up, meaning the game had already been quietly cooking for roughly seven years by the time it launched in 2015. Lead artist Istvan Pely stuck with the Fallout concept work rather than moving onto Skyrim with the rest of the team.

title: Porting Skyrim Just To Learn The Hardware
description: Before building any of Fallout 4 itself, the team's first move on the new console hardware was porting Skyrim to the Xbox One, purely as a way of learning the console's capabilities and figuring out the new renderer they'd need. Todd Howard has joked that fans shouldn't get too excited about that particular port.

title: The Writer's Childhood Bedroom
description: Lead writer Emil Pagliarulo grew up in Boston, and once the city was locked in as Fallout 4's setting, he couldn't resist putting a bit of himself into the game. One of the destroyed houses you can wander through is modeled on his actual childhood bedroom, complete with a mattress buried under a pile of comic books.

title: The Vault 75 UFO Crash
description: Head to Vault 75 and you can trigger one of the game's hidden UFO encounters, complete with an alien crash site to fight through. Win the scrap and you'll walk away with an alien blaster pistol, easily one of the most satisfying secret weapons to stumble across in the Commonwealth.

title: A Quiet Tribute to Daniel Kinnard
description: In the farmhouse near the end of the game, when Joel and Tommy are combing the place for Ellie, there's a baseball poster tucked away in one of the rooms featuring a face fans might not recognise straight away - Daniel Kinnard. He was a Naughty Dog developer who sadly passed away while the remake was being made, and the studio quietly wrote him into the world as a lasting nod to his work.

title: Justin Bieber, Movie Star
description: Scattered copies of a fictional newspaper called The Daily Metro pop up across the game, and if you stop to actually read the headlines, one of them is a proper gem: 'Uncharted 13: A Lush Movie — Justin Bieber as Drake.' Naughty Dog poking a bit of fun at their own flagship franchise.

title: Ellie's Kill Bill Jumpsuit
description: Once you've finished the game and unlocked some of the cosmetic outfits, one option for Ellie is a bright yellow tracksuit that's unmistakably lifted from Uma Thurman's Bride in Kill Bill. Given how far Ellie's come by the credits, it's a fitting look for her.

title: O'Sullivan's Pub
description: There's a rundown pub you pass through called O'Sullivan's, and the layout is a deliberate callback to the bar brawl that kicks off Uncharted 3. The name itself is a nod to Victor 'Sully' Sullivan, Nathan Drake's long-time partner in crime.

title: Run, You're Nearly There
description: During the grim final stretch through the Firefly hospital, keep an eye on the eye test charts hanging on the walls. One of them isn't random letters at all - it spells out 'RUN YOU R NEARLY THERE DON'T QUIT!!', a bit of dark encouragement for players white-knuckling their way to the ending.

title: Clementine's House Makes an Appearance
description: While exploring with Bill, you'll pass a house that looks strikingly familiar if you've played Telltale's The Walking Dead - it's built to resemble Clementine's home from the very start of that game, just left to rot a little longer. A nice bit of respect between two of the era's best story-driven survival games.

title: Plushies of PlayStation Royalty
description: In Serenity Apartments, right after you meet Henry and Sam, take a look around the bedroom - there's a Jak & Daxter plush on the dresser and a Nathan Drake plushie on the bed. The remake even throws in a second Drake plush for good measure.

title: PS3s Hidden in Plain Sight
description: Since the original game launched on PlayStation 3, Naughty Dog snuck actual PS3 consoles into the environment as a little in-joke. You can spot one under Joel and Sarah's TV right at the start, and another later inside Larry's TV & Stereo store, complete with a couple of DualShock controllers on a nearby shelf.

title: The Faithful Dog
description: Naughty Dog isn't shy about referencing itself - in Pittsburgh you'll come across a poster for the official Last of Us website and a mousepad bearing the studio's logo. There's also a pet store called Faithful Dog, a pun that's hard to miss once you notice it.

title: A Glimpse of What's Next?
description: Not long after the remake launched, fans started sharing screenshots of a pinboard covered in fantasy-style concept art, including what looks like a unicorn-esque creature. Similar imagery had already turned up in The Last of Us Part II, and plenty of players are convinced it's a breadcrumb pointing toward Naughty Dog's next original IP.

title: Dawn of the Wolf
description: A movie poster for 'Dawn of the Wolf' shows up first in Sarah's bedroom and then keeps resurfacing in different variations throughout the game. It's a not-so-subtle jab at the Twilight saga, right down to the moody romantic tagline.

title: Mortal Kombat on the Wall
description: Right at the start of the game, in Sarah's room, there's a poster for Mortal Kombat II tucked among the other decorations. The kind of detail you'd only catch if you slow down and actually look at a teenager's bedroom instead of rushing to the next objective.

title: Fake Bands, Real Parodies
description: The Marquis Music Store in Bill's Town is stacked with fictional album covers that are clearly winking at real bands - 'Into the Breach' by the Blaggard Boys riffs on AC/DC's 'For Those About to Rock,' while 'Unidentified Objects' by FULLFUNK mirrors Parliament's 'Mothership Connection.' A fun little detour for anyone who actually stops to browse the shelves.

title: Bill's Letter, Flipped
description: In the game, Joel finds a devastating note written by Frank to Bill before Frank takes his own life. The HBO show flips the whole scene around - it's Bill who leaves the letter, addressed to whoever finds his house after he and Frank die together. Same heartbreak, told from the opposite direction.

title: It Was Almost a Jak and Daxter Game
description: Before Joel and Ellie ever existed, Naughty Dog had been kicking around ideas for a new Jak and Daxter entry, even producing concept art of a photorealistic Jak. The team eventually admitted they weren't passionate about making it just because it was an easy sell, so their bosses told them to go build whatever they actually wanted instead - and The Last of Us was the result.

title: One Studio, Split in Two
description: After Uncharted 2 wrapped up in 2009, Naughty Dog didn't just move on to another sequel - they split into two teams. One half stayed on Uncharted duty for Drake's Deception, while the other half went off to build something completely new, which eventually became The Last of Us.

title: Joel and Ellie Didn't Always Have Last Names
description: Early on, the working names for the leads were Joel 'Miller' and Ellie 'Williams,' but Naughty Dog dropped surnames entirely for the finished 2013 game. Fans kept using the old names anyway, and eventually the studio made it official - 'Miller' was confirmed as canon in Part II, and Neil Druckmann later confirmed 'Williams' for Ellie himself.

title: The Clicks Are Made by Real People
description: That spine-chilling clicking sound the Clickers make isn't some purely digital effect - it starts with live voice actors physically performing the noise. Misty Lee, who's provided clicking for both the game and the HBO adaptation, has spoken about the process, and once you know real vocal cords are behind it, it somehow gets creepier.

title: The Remake Started at a Different Studio
description: Before Naughty Dog ever touched it, the Part I remake was quietly being built by Sony's Visual Arts Service Group, a support studio better known for helping finish other people's games. Sony eventually pulled the project and handed it to Naughty Dog outright, which led to a fair bit of frustration - and several departures - from the original team.

title: Different Roles for the Original Joel and Ellie
description: Troy Baker and Ashley Johnson, the voices behind Joel and Ellie in the games, both turn up in the HBO series - just not as Joel and Ellie. Baker plays James, part of David's group in season one, while Johnson appears as Anna, Ellie's mother, giving longtime fans a proper nod without any recasting confusion.

title: Troy Baker Almost Walked Away from Joel
description: Troy Baker has admitted he nearly left his own audition for Joel because he didn't feel like he was right for the part. Neil Druckmann clearly disagreed, and once Baker and Ashley Johnson started reading together, the chemistry that ended up defining the whole game was already there.

title: Ashley Johnson's Double BAFTA
description: Ashley Johnson didn't just voice Ellie once and move on - she picked up BAFTA Award wins for her performance in both the original game and the Left Behind expansion. Part of why fans were so invested in seeing her get a meaningful role when the HBO show came around.

title: The Bank Vault Ring
description: Poke around the vault in the Seattle bank during Day 1 downtown and you'll find a drawer with an engraved ring sitting inside it. It's the same ring Nathan Drake wears throughout the Uncharted series, a nice little wink from Naughty Dog to their other flagship franchise.

title: A Precursor Orb in the Rubble
description: Tucked away among the debris in one of the exploration-heavy Seattle areas is a glowing orb that looks suspiciously familiar to anyone who grew up with Naughty Dog's earlier platformer series. It's a straight-up reference to the Precursor Orbs collected throughout the Jak and Daxter games.

title: A Handheld From Another Naughty Dog Universe
description: One of the more surprising finds scattered through Part 2's abandoned buildings is a battered handheld console displaying Hotline Miami's neon-drenched box art. It's a small crossover nod to Dennaton Games' brutal top-down shooter, hiding in a game that's just as violent in its own way.

title: Dressed as Nathan Drake
description: Among the various costumes and outfits players can dig up during their scavenging runs is a full Nathan Drake Halloween getup. It's become one of the most talked-about crossover finds in the whole game, mostly because it looks ridiculous on Ellie.

title: The Door Code Every Immersive Sim Fan Knows
description: The code to unlock Gate West 2 during the Seattle sections is 0451, a number that's basically folklore among PC gaming veterans. It traces back to a door code at Looking Glass Studios' old Cambridge office and has been quietly slipped into games like System Shock and Thief ever since.

title: A Battered Copy of The Velveteen Rabbit
description: Wander into the Seattle bookshop and you can spot a worn copy of the 1922 children's classic The Velveteen Rabbit sitting on a shelf. It's an odd little detail to include in a game this grim, and fans reckon it's a personal touch from someone on the dev team rather than a storyline nod.

title: The Sic Parvis Magna Ring and a Point Break Chat
description: During the same scene where Ellie picks up a ring engraved with 'Sic Parvis Magna,' another Uncharted callback, she and Dina end up chatting about Point Break, the 1991 bank-heist movie with Keanu Reeves and Patrick Swayze. Two references stacked into one quiet conversation.

title: Ellie Finally Learned to Swim
description: Anyone who played the original game remembers the running gag that Ellie couldn't swim, which led to some clunky pallet-pushing puzzles. Naughty Dog leaned right into it here: swim over to a pallet by the museum and Ellie cracks a joke about Joel once having to shove her across the water like that.

title: Sam's Toy Robot Makes a Comeback
description: Fans of the first game still think fondly of Sam and Henry, the brothers Joel and Ellie travel with for a stretch. In a quiet moment in Part 2, Ellie comes across Sam's old toy robot and picks it up, a small gesture that carries a surprising amount of weight if you remember how their story ended.

title: That Guitar Isn't Just for Show
description: Naughty Dog built such a detailed guitar-playing system for Ellie that players quickly figured out they could recreate actual songs on it, note for note, using the touchpad to strum and a chord wheel to fret. People have pulled off everything from Nirvana to Metallica to a fingerpicked take on A-ha's Take On Me, all without a single line of code being changed.

title: Curtis and Viper 2
description: Somewhere in Part 2's dialogue, Joel and Ellie bond over a fictional action-movie franchise called Curtis and Viper 2, a series that only exists inside this world. It clearly meant something to the writers too, because the HBO adaptation brought the same made-up franchise back when Dina mentions wanting to watch it with Joel.

title: Why Ellie Loves the Stars
description: Joel gifting Ellie an astronomy book isn't just a sentimental prop. Neil Druckmann has said the whole detail exists because Ashley Johnson, who plays Ellie, wanted to be an astronaut as a kid. In the same breath, he's explained that Joel's love of music and singing comes from the fact that Troy Baker started out as an actual musician before he ever voiced a video game character.

title: The Tattoo Story That Almost Made the Cut
description: There's a cut sequence called Jackson Party that was trimmed from the finished game but resurfaced as one of the Lost Levels in the remaster. It shows Ellie more settled into her life before everything falls apart, including a scene that finally explains where her tattoo actually came from.

title: A New Director's Chair
description: Bruce Straley, who co-directed the original game alongside Neil Druckmann, left Naughty Dog in 2017 and had no involvement in the sequel. His shoes were filled by Anthony Newman and Kurt Margenau, with Newman having previously worked as the melee combat designer on the first game.

title: No Factions Here, On Purpose
description: The multiplayer mode Factions was a genuine fan favourite from the first game, but Naughty Dog made a deliberate call to leave it out of Part 2 entirely so the whole team could pour every ounce of effort into the single-player campaign. They were clear that Factions wasn't gone for good, just parked for a while.

title: Most Awarded Game Ever Made
description: By the time all the dust settled on the 2020 awards season, The Last of Us Part 2 had picked up more Game of the Year wins than any other game in history, knocking The Witcher 3 off the top spot it had held for years.

title: Over 60 Ways to Play It Your Way
description: This game shipped with more than 60 individual accessibility settings, covering everything from custom button remapping to on-screen cues for hard-of-hearing players. It went on to win the very first Innovation in Accessibility award handed out at The Game Awards, a category that basically got created because of how far Naughty Dog pushed things.

title: Over Two Thousand People Built This Game
description: Naughty Dog's own team sits at around 350 people, but the finished game credits roughly 2,169 developers spread across 14 different studios who chipped in on everything from animation to localisation over the years it took to make.

title: Four Million Copies Before the Weekend Was Over
description: This was easily the biggest launch of 2020 across both physical and digital sales, moving over four million copies in its opening weekend alone and becoming the fastest-selling PlayStation 4 exclusive of all time.

title: The Leak That Turned Ugly
description: Months before release, huge chunks of the story and cutscenes leaked online, and the fallout was genuinely nasty. Abby's voice actress Laura Bailey ended up receiving death threats aimed at her newborn son, serious enough that some had to be passed along to authorities, and Abby's face model Jocelyn Mettler was reportedly still fielding hate mail years after the game came out.

title: No Return Throws Everything at You at Once
description: The 2024 PS5 remaster added a roguelike mode called No Return, where you fight through randomised encounters as one of ten unlockable characters, including Joel, Tommy, Dina, and even a couple of names from Abby's side of the story. Each character controls a bit differently, so runs never quite feel the same twice.

title: Three Levels That Never Made It Out
description: Tucked into the remaster are three Lost Levels, unfinished early builds of sections that got cut from the final game, complete with developer commentary explaining why certain ideas didn't survive. Interestingly, all three belong to Ellie's story, so anything that got trimmed from Abby's side is still a mystery.

title: It Was Never Meant to Be a Full Game
description: ODST started life as a scrappy little side project called Halo 3: Recon, something Bungie figured they'd knock out quickly to fill the gap before Halo: Reach. Then-CEO Harold Ryan basically told Joe Staten and Paul Bertone to build it fast using the existing Halo 3 engine, with zero extra engineering support. It grew arms and legs along the way and turned into a full retail release.

title: A Detective Story Wearing a Halo Skin
description: Rather than another straight-line Spartan shooting gallery, Joe Staten pitched ODST as film noir: a lone soldier wandering a rain-soaked, ruined city piecing together what happened to his squad through flashbacks. It's basically a detective mystery wrapped in Covenant armour, which is a big part of why it still feels different from every other Halo campaign.

title: Firefly's Cast Basically Reunited on New Mombasa
description: Three of your five squadmates are played by former Firefly cast members. Nathan Fillion (Captain Mal himself) voices Buck, Adam Baldwin plays Dutch, and Alan Tudyk voices Mickey. Romeo's the odd one out, but if ODST's banter ever felt weirdly like eavesdropping on the Serenity crew, that's why.

title: Number Six Is Running Your Squad
description: Veronica Dare, the ONI officer who takes command of the squad before the drop, is voiced by Tricia Helfer. Sci-fi fans will know her better as Number Six from the rebooted Battlestar Galactica, so ODST quietly doubles as a bit of a genre casting crossover.

title: Joe Staten Talks to Himself the Whole Game
description: Lead writer Joseph Staten has voiced every single Grunt in the Halo trilogy, but in ODST he also stepped in to voice the New Mombasa Superintendent, the calm AI narrating the Rookie's wander through the city. So a fair chunk of the game's dialogue, both the smallest alien mooks and the biggest guiding voice, comes out of the same guy.

title: The Score Traded Orchestras for a Jazz Club
description: Martin O'Donnell and Michael Salvatori threw out Halo's usual sweeping choral sound for ODST and went moody and jazz-inflected instead, all rain-slicked saxophone and quiet piano. It fits the noir detective angle so well that the soundtrack is still one of the most-praised things about the whole game.

title: ODST Doctrine Was Basically Ripped from Starship Troopers
description: Halo's always worn its Starship Troopers influence on its sleeve, but ODST leans in hardest. The orbital drop pods echo the Mobile Infantry's capsule drops from Heinlein's novel and Verhoeven's film, and the ODST rule of sending commanding officers down first mirrors the Mobile Infantry's own 'officers first' doctrine.

title: Buck's Secret Encounter with an Old Friend
description: During the epilogue, right as Vergil lights up Sergeant Johnson's cigar, nudge the right stick to the left and the camera drifts off to the side. You'll catch Buck crouched next to what looks like an ape, grooming it and, well, eating something out of its fur before the screen cuts to black. Look closer and that creature is wearing the face of Halo art director Marcus Lehto, the same joke used for the cavemen back in Halo 3's Sierra 117.

title: There's a Dancing Man Hidden in a Firefight Map
description: Tucked off to the side of one of the open Firefight areas, away from the main fighting, is a strange little figure doing a dance loop that nobody in the story ever acknowledges. Players have long taken it as a cheeky nod to Bungie's audio director Martin O'Donnell, one of those in-jokes the team slipped in purely for the fans who go looking off the beaten path.

title: Vergil Isn't Just a Random Name
description: The AI subroutine that watches over Sadie throughout her half of the story is called Vergil, and that's a direct pull from Dante's Inferno, where the poet Virgil guides Dante through the circles of hell. In Sadie's Story, Vergil plays much the same role, steering Sadie and Mike (and eventually the Rookie) through a New Mombasa that's very deliberately structured like Dante's descent.

title: Sadie's Story Ran on Its Own Website Too
description: The 30 audio logs scattered around Mombasa Streets weren't just an in-game collectible. Studio Fourth Wall built Sadie's Story as a companion alternate reality experience on Bungie.net, complete with the same illustrated slideshows, so fans could follow Sadie's side of the invasion outside the game entirely. Bungie.net is long gone now, but the whole thing still survives on the Wayback Machine.

title: The Butcher in the Casino District Has a Name Too
description: Every one of the Inferno's circles gets mapped onto a chunk of New Mombasa in Sadie's Story: Gluttony belongs to a hulking butcher named Jonas handing out food while the city falls apart around him, and Avarice is the casino district being looted blind. It's a small detail, but once you notice the Dante structure the whole audio log trail reads completely differently.

title: Firefight Owes Gears of War a Drink
description: ODST's wave-based Firefight mode is Bungie's own spin on the Horde mode Epic had introduced in Gears of War 2 the year before. It went on to become one of ODST's most enduring contributions to the series, sticking around in nearly every mainline Halo game that followed.

title: A Police-Themed Unlock Got Quietly Pulled
description: When 343 built ODST's Master Chief Collection season, they'd originally planned an unlockable nameplate styled after an NMPD police lightbar, tying into the city police force you run into throughout the campaign. It got cut before launch out of sensitivity to the real-world conversations happening around policing at the time, in 2020.

title: That Screaming Marine Has Shown Up Before
description: In Uplift Reserve you'll find a Warthog with a medic trying to calm down a marine who's completely losing it. That's the same panicking soldier from the Floodgate level in Halo 3, so if his reaction feels oddly specific for a random NPC, it's because he's already had one very bad day before this one.

title: A Developer Photobombed His Own Game
description: Somewhere in ODST there's a framed photo meant to be the Rookie's girlfriend, and the picture used is actually an edited shot of Bungie developer Chris Butcher. It's the kind of joke that only really gets explained once you know the studio well enough to recognize the face.

title: Sadie Almost Had a Different Name
description: Sadie Endesha was originally written as Maddie. The name got changed late because a marketing trailer used the line 'Maddie, where are you,' and someone realized it landed way too close to a certain unrelated pop culture reference for comfort, so the team swapped it before launch to avoid the coincidence.

title: ODST Sold More Than Anything Else on Xbox 360 That Year
description: Despite being pitched internally as a smaller side story rather than a mainline sequel, ODST launched as the best-selling Xbox 360 game worldwide, proving there was plenty of appetite for a quieter, character-driven Halo story even without Master Chief front and centre.

title: New Mombasa Is a Real Place, Rebuilt for the Future
description: The ruined city you spend the whole campaign creeping through is a reimagined, futurized version of the actual Kenyan port city of Mombasa. Bungie's art team used it as the canvas for the invasion, which is part of why ODST's setting feels so much more grounded and lived-in than the alien ringworlds and installations the series usually deals in.

title: The Rookie Is the Only Playable ODST in the Series
description: Every other mainline Halo game hands you a Spartan, but ODST is the one time the series lets you play as a regular, mortal soldier instead. The Rookie never says a word the entire game, and he's the character you both start and end the story with, wandering the streets between everyone else's flashbacks.

title: The Glyphs Nobody Could Crack for Years
description: Scattered through ODST are strange glyph symbols that fans spent years trying to decode, convinced they hid some kind of message or code left by Bungie. Community sleuths kept chasing the mystery well over a decade after release, with Marty O'Donnell himself eventually dropping hints, making it one of the longest-running unsolved secrets tied to the game.

title: Recon Never Fully Went Away
description: Even after the game was renamed from Halo 3: Recon to Halo 3: ODST, the old title stuck around in small ways. When 343 built the Master Chief Collection season around ODST, they named it 'Recon' and gave the game's era-specific weapon set the same name, a little nod back to what it was almost called.

title: One Disc, Two Games' Worth of Multiplayer
description: ODST didn't just ship with its own campaign and Firefight mode, it also included the entirety of Halo 3's multiplayer on a separate disc in the box. New copies even came with access codes for the Halo: Reach multiplayer beta, so buying ODST effectively bought you a foot in the door for Bungie's next game too.

title: Following the Alarms and Sirens Is the Whole Trick
description: There's no marker pointing straight at ODST's 30 audio logs. Instead the city itself tips you off, car alarms blaring, payphones ringing, street barriers lifting for no reason, all of it stops the second you're near a terminal you haven't found yet. It's a subtle way of making an open, mostly empty city feel like it's still quietly reacting to you.

title: The Superintendent Wrote Its Own Babysitter
description: Vergil isn't an independent AI, it's a subroutine that Sadie's own father, Dr. Daniel Endesha, coded specifically to keep an eye on his daughter while he worked at the Superintendent's data centre. So the AI that ends up guiding half the game's story exists purely because one dad wanted a way to make sure his kid didn't skip town unsupervised.

title: A Character Named After a Circle of Hell
description: Tom Uberti, one of the figures in Sadie's Story, seems to be a nod to Dante's Farinata degli Uberti, a heretic condemned to spend eternity trapped in a burning tomb. Tom's own fate in the story mirrors that fairly closely, which fits given how heavily the whole audio log arc leans on Inferno imagery.
